title: Steering through air: drag, balance and control in flight

summary.text: A raindrop can fall from a cloud a kilometre up, yet it lands at no more than about 30 kilometres an hour. Why does it stop speeding up? The air pushes back on anything that moves through it, and pushes harder the faster the thing goes. Your child races parachutes, steers paper planes by bending their wings, and watches smoke whirl behind a card. They find out why shape matters, why a shuttlecock always lands cork first, how flyers turn, and why geese take turns at the front of a line.
summary.art: A grey monsoon sky over a rooftop in Chennai: a long raindrop falling, a parachute made from a polythene bag floating down with a coin, and a line of flamingos crossing the clouds.

intro.hook: Hold a flat card in front of your chest and walk fast across the room. Feel the card push back. Now turn the card edge-on and walk again. The card is the same, and you walk at the same speed. What changed?
intro.text: Nothing changed except how much of the card faces the air. Air is a real material, and a moving thing has to push it out of the way. The air pushes back. That push is called drag, and flyers spend most of their effort fighting it, using it and steering with it. In this unit you race parachutes, bend paper wings to steer, and watch what a moving card leaves behind in the air.
intro.art: A girl walking across a room holding a flat card in front of her chest, with small arrows showing air pushing back on the card, and next to her the same card turned edge-on with almost no arrows.

outcomes: I can explain drag as the push of air against a moving thing, and say what makes it bigger: speed, size facing the air, and shape.
I can explain why a falling thing stops speeding up, and why a parachute slows a fall.
I can run a fair test that changes one thing at a time, repeat each drop three times and use the average.
I can explain why a plane, a shuttlecock or an arrow flies straight, using the balance point and the tail.
I can explain how a flyer turns by changing the lift on one wing, and name pitch, roll and yaw.
I can explain how flying in a line saves energy, and how the air a flyer moves goes on moving after she has passed.
I can explain why small things fall gently, and why a jet flies high where the air is thin.

terms.meaning: The push of air against anything that moves through it. Drag always pushes against the direction of motion.
terms.example: You feel drag when you open an umbrella and run into the wind.
terms.art: A girl running with an open umbrella, with arrows showing the air pushing back on the umbrella.

terms.meaning: Another name for drag when the air is the thing pushing back.
terms.example: Air resistance slows a paper ball more slowly than a flat sheet of paper.
terms.art: A flat sheet of paper and a paper ball falling side by side, with the flat sheet falling more slowly.

terms.meaning: Shaped so that air flows smoothly round it: round at the front, with a long, gentle slope at the back.
terms.example: A fish, a bullet train and a kingfisher's beak are streamlined.
terms.art: A teardrop shape with smooth lines of air flowing round it and closing neatly behind.

terms.meaning: The moving, swirling air or water left behind a thing that has moved through it.
terms.example: A boat leaves a wake of waves, and a lorry leaves a wake of swirling air.
terms.art: A boat on a river with a V of waves spreading out behind it.

terms.meaning: The top speed of a falling thing, reached when drag has grown as big as its weight. After that it stops speeding up.
terms.example: A big raindrop reaches a terminal speed of about 9 metres each second.
terms.art: A raindrop falling, with a down arrow for weight and an up arrow for drag of the same length.

terms.meaning: The wide cloth part of a parachute that catches the air.
terms.example: The canopy of a skydiver's parachute is bigger than a room.
terms.art: A parachute with its round canopy open and a person hanging below on strings.

terms.meaning: The one spot where a thing balances. Scientists call it the centre of gravity. The whole weight of the thing seems to act there.
terms.example: A ruler balances on your finger at its middle.
terms.art: A paper plane balanced on a fingertip, with a dot showing the balance point.

terms.meaning: Stable means that after a small bump, the flyer swings back to flying straight by itself.
terms.example: A shuttlecock thrown sideways turns itself round to fly cork first.
terms.art: A paper plane wobbling nose-up, then a curved arrow showing it dipping back to level.

terms.meaning: When the nose of a plane tips up or down.
terms.example: A plane pitches up as it starts to climb after take-off.
terms.art: A side view of a plane with a curved arrow showing the nose tipping up.

terms.meaning: When a plane tilts to one side, with one wing going down and the other going up.
terms.example: A plane rolls left before it turns left.
terms.art: A plane seen from the front with a curved arrow showing the wings tilting.

terms.meaning: When the nose of a plane swings left or right, like a door turning on its hinge.
terms.example: A boat yaws when you turn its rudder.
terms.art: A plane seen from above with a curved arrow showing the nose swinging to one side.

terms.meaning: A flap on the tail of a plane that tips the nose up or down.
terms.example: Pilots tilt the elevator up to make the nose rise.
terms.art: The tail of a plane with a flap bent up and an arrow showing the tail pushed down.

terms.meaning: A flap on the back edge of each wing. One goes up while the other goes down, to roll the plane.
terms.example: To roll left, the left aileron goes up and the right aileron goes down.
terms.art: A plane seen from behind with its left aileron up and its right aileron down.

terms.meaning: An upright flap on the tail that swings the nose left or right.
terms.example: A boat and a plane both have a rudder.
terms.art: The upright tail fin of a plane with its rudder turned to one side.

terms.meaning: To lean a plane over to one side, with its wings tilted, so that it turns.
terms.example: A cyclist leans into a bend in the same way.
terms.art: A plane flying a curve with its wings tilted, next to a cyclist leaning into a bend.

terms.meaning: Air that is pushed upwards behind the wing tip of a flying bird or plane.
terms.example: A bird flying just behind and beside another can ride on her upwash.
terms.art: Two birds flying one behind the other, with small arrows showing air rising beside the front bird's wing tip.

terms.meaning: How much air is packed into a space. High up, the air is less dense, so it is thinner.
terms.example: The air on top of a mountain is thinner than the air in Chennai.
terms.art: Two boxes of the same size, one full of dots for sea-level air and one with only a few dots for air on a mountain top.

terms.meaning: An instrument that measures how fast the wind blows. Many have little cups that spin in the wind.
terms.example: Weather stations use an anemometer on a tall pole.
terms.art: A weather-station pole with three spinning cups on top.

explanations.concept: Drag: the air pushes back on anything that moves through it
explanations.definition: Drag is the push of air against a thing that moves through it. It pushes against the direction the thing is moving.
explanations.description: Air is made of countless tiny particles called molecules. A moving thing has to shove those molecules out of the way, and they push back. You feel this when you run with an open umbrella. You also feel it when you hold a card flat in front of you and walk, and it does not push back much when you turn the card edge-on. Three things decide how big the drag is. The first is speed. The second is how much of the thing faces the air. The third is shape. A thing that goes straight through at a steady speed has drag exactly equal to the push that drives it. That is why a cyclist keeps pedalling to hold the same speed.
examples: A flat card walked through the air pushes back much harder than the same card turned edge-on.
A cyclist pedals only to cancel the drag, once she is up to speed.
An open umbrella pulls hard against the wind, and a closed one hardly does.
explanations.art: A cyclist leaning forward with arrows showing air pushing back on her body and an equal arrow forward from the pedals.

explanations.concept: Speed matters a lot: twice as fast, about four times the drag
explanations.definition: For most everyday speeds, drag grows with the square of the speed. Twice as fast gives about four times the drag.
explanations.description: When you go twice as fast, you meet twice as much air every second. And you hit each bit of it twice as hard. Two times two is four. Three times as fast gives three times three, which is nine times the drag. This is why riding into the wind on a cycle feels so hard, and why a car at 100 kilometres an hour uses much more fuel than at 50. A jet at full speed spends nearly all of its engine push just fighting drag. In steady, level flight, thrust equals drag, and lift equals weight. All four forces are balanced, and the plane flies straight at a steady speed.
examples: A cyclist at 20 kilometres an hour feels about four times the air push she feels at 10.
A car at 100 kilometres an hour has about four times the drag it has at 50.
A jet in level flight has thrust equal to drag and lift equal to weight.
explanations.art: A bar chart of drag at speeds 10, 20 and 30 kilometres an hour, with bars of height 1, 4 and 9.

explanations.concept: Why a falling thing stops speeding up: terminal speed
explanations.definition: A falling thing speeds up until its drag equals its weight. After that it falls at a steady speed called its terminal speed.
explanations.description: When you let go, only weight is pulling the thing down, so it speeds up. As it speeds up, drag grows. At some speed the drag grows as big as the weight. Then the forces are balanced, and the thing stops speeding up. A big raindrop falls at no more than about 9 metres each second, or about 30 kilometres an hour, though it may fall from a cloud a kilometre up. A parachute has a huge canopy, so it reaches the balance at a very low speed. A heavier thing needs more drag to balance it, so it falls faster. But four times the weight does not make four times the speed. It makes about two times the speed. A skydiver falling flat reaches about 55 metres each second, and a skydiver with a parachute open lands at about 5.
examples: A big raindrop stops speeding up at about 9 metres each second.
A skydiver falling belly-down reaches about 55 metres each second, about 200 kilometres an hour.
A skydiver tucked head-down falls faster than one with her arms spread out.
explanations.art: A falling raindrop at three heights, with a down arrow for weight that stays the same and an up arrow for drag that grows until the two arrows are equal.

explanations.concept: Shape and streamlining: where drag comes from
explanations.definition: A streamlined shape has a rounded front and a long, gentle slope behind. Air flows smoothly round it and closes up neatly behind, leaving a small wake.
explanations.description: Drag has two main sources. The first is the air being shoved aside. Behind a blunt shape such as a flat plate, the air cannot close up smoothly. It breaks into a big, messy wake, and the low pressure in that wake pulls the shape back. The second source is that air sticks a little to any surface. A thin layer of air clings to the skin of a plane, a fish or a card, and rubs against the air moving past. A teardrop shape can have more than ten times less drag than a flat disc of the same width. This is why fish, birds, bullet trains and planes are rounded in front and tapered behind. A pointed front is not what matters. The slope of the back matters more.
examples: The nose of Japan's 500 Series bullet train was shaped like a kingfisher's beak, to cut drag and noise.
A tuna and a cheel both have smooth, tapered bodies.
A cyclist crouched low, in a smooth helmet, has less drag than one sitting upright.
explanations.art: A flat plate and a teardrop of the same width in a stream of air, with the plate leaving a big swirling wake and the teardrop leaving a thin one.

explanations.concept: Thin air: why jets fly high
explanations.definition: Air gets thinner with height. At the height where jets cruise, the air is about a third as dense as it is near the ground.
explanations.description: The air near the ground is squashed by all the air above it. Higher up there is less air above, so the air is less squashed and has fewer molecules in each cubic metre. At 10 kilometres the air is about one third as dense as at the ground. On the top of Mount Everest the air is thinner still, and climbers often carry oxygen. Thin air means less drag, so a jet burns less fuel at the same speed. It also means less lift, so the wings must move faster through the air. That is why a jet cruises at about 900 kilometres an hour high up, and lands at about 250. In 2012, Felix Baumgartner jumped from a balloon 39 kilometres up. In the very thin air there he reached about 1,357 kilometres an hour before the thicker air slowed him.
examples: A jet cruises about 10 kilometres up, where the air is about a third as dense.
Bar-headed geese cross the high Himalayas on their way to India, in air much thinner than at the sea.
Baumgartner fell faster than sound because the air at 39 kilometres up is so thin.
explanations.art: A tall column of air from the ground to the sky, with many dots at the bottom and fewer dots higher up, and a jet at the height where the dots are few.

explanations.concept: Why a flyer flies straight: the balance point and the tail
explanations.definition: A flyer is stable when a small bump makes forces that turn it back to where it was. A tail and a balance point near the front make a plane stable.
explanations.description: The balance point is the spot where the weight of a plane seems to act. If it is a little ahead of where the wing's lift acts, the nose tends to drop back down after a bump. The tail helps too. A tail is a small wing. If a bump tips the nose up, the tail swings down and meets the air at a steeper angle. The air pushes the tail up, and the nose dips back to level. A shuttlecock works in a similar way. It has a heavy cork head and a skirt of feathers with much more drag. If it flies tail-first, the drag on the feathers swings them round behind. An arrow's feathers and a kite's tail do the same job. But there is a trade-off. A very stable plane is hard to turn. Fighter jets are made less stable on purpose, and computers help the pilot keep them steady.
examples: A shuttlecock hit sideways turns itself round to fly cork first.
An arrow flies straight because of its feathers at the back.
A kite with no tail twirls and dives, and a longer tail steadies it.
explanations.art: Side view of a paper plane with its nose tipped up, a small arrow pushing the tail up, and a curved arrow showing the nose coming back down.

explanations.concept: How a flyer turns: pitch, roll and yaw
explanations.definition: A flyer can tip its nose up and down (pitch), tilt its wings (roll) and swing its nose left and right (yaw). It does these by changing the lift on parts of its wings and tail.
explanations.description: A flap on the back edge of a wing changes how much air that part of the wing pushes down. Bend a flap down, and that part of the wing pushes more air down and lifts more. Bend it up, and it lifts less. The elevator on the tail tips the nose up or down. The ailerons on the wings work in opposite ways, one up and one down, so that one wing lifts more than the other. The wing that lifts less goes down, and the plane rolls. Once it is tilted, some of the lift pulls the plane sideways, and the plane goes round a curve. This is called banking. A cyclist leans into a bend in the same way. The rudder only fine-tunes the turn. Birds do the same. They twist their wings and fan or tilt their tails.
examples: A pilot rolls left by raising the left aileron and lowering the right one.
A crow spreads and tilts her tail when she lands, so that she slows and steers.
A cyclist leans into a bend, and a plane banks into a turn.
explanations.art: Three small planes: one with its nose pitching up, one rolling with its wings tilted, and one yawing with its nose turned to the side, each with a curved arrow.

explanations.concept: Flying in each other's air: wakes and the V
explanations.definition: A flyer leaves moving air behind. A bird that flies in the right place can be lifted by that air and save energy.
explanations.description: A wing makes lift by pushing air down. Behind the wing tips, the air curls round into two spinning whirls. Outside the wing tips, that air goes up. This rising air is called upwash. A bird that flies just behind and to the side of another can be lifted by her. In 2014, scientists put tiny trackers on northern bald ibises that were flying in a V behind a microlight. They found that each ibis put her wing tip in the right place, and flapped in step with the bird ahead to catch the upwash. In 2001, researchers measured the heartbeat of great white pelicans flying in a line and found it was slower than when they flew alone. Early sums from 1970 said a big V could save a great deal of energy. Measurements on live birds find smaller savings, but still real. Cyclists use the same idea when they follow in a line.
examples: Ibises flapping in step with the bird ahead to catch her upwash.
Cyclists riding in a line, taking turns at the front.
Flamingos and geese flying in a V or a long slanting line.
explanations.art: A V of geese seen from above, with small curved arrows showing air rising just outside the wing tip of each bird.

perspectives.explanation: Birds in a V place themselves and time their flaps to catch the upwash of the bird ahead, and so save energy.

A V also lets every bird see the others and keep in touch, so the shape may be partly about seeing and keeping together. How much is energy and how much is seeing may be different for each kind of bird.

explanations.concept: Small things fall gently: size and surface
explanations.definition: A small animal has more skin for each bit of weight than a big one, so air slows her fall far more.
explanations.description: Imagine an animal twice as long, twice as tall and twice as wide. It has 4 times as much skin, but 8 times as much weight. So a bigger body has less skin for each bit of weight, and the air slows it less. In 1926, the biologist J. B. S. Haldane wrote that a mouse can fall down a deep mine shaft and walk away, while a person would be badly hurt. Haldane later moved to India, in 1957. A tiny insect has so much skin for her weight that she floats down like dust. This is also why you saw the small, light seed spinners fall slowly, and why big birds must flap harder than small ones. For a very small flyer, air feels thick, like water does for us. Tiny wasps have wings like feathers, made of fine bristles, and they seem to swim through the air.
examples: A mouse can survive a fall that would badly hurt a person.
An ant falls from a table and walks away, because drag slows her fast.
Tiny wasps have bristly wings that push through air which feels thick to them.
explanations.art: A mouse and an elephant falling side by side, the mouse landing gently and the elephant landing hard, with small arrows showing air pushing against each.

explanations.concept: Where flight ends: no air, no drag and no wings
explanations.definition: Without air there is no drag and no lift. Wings and flaps do nothing. A spacecraft steers by pushing on its own exhaust.
explanations.description: Above about 100 kilometres, the air is so thin that wings cannot make lift. A rocket pushes out burning gas, and the gas pushes the rocket the other way. When a spacecraft comes back, it hits the air at about 28,000 kilometres an hour. Drag is so strong that it turns the spacecraft's motion into heat. A shield on the front takes the heat. India's capsule SRE-1 came back this way in January 2007 and landed in the Bay of Bengal. Shooting stars glow for the same reason. Tiny bits of rock hit the air so fast that they heat up and burn. So drag does not only slow things down. It changes motion into warmth. The energy is not lost. It becomes the heat of the air and the shield.
examples: A shooting star is a bit of rock heated by drag as it hits the air.
A returning capsule has a heat shield on its front.
On the Moon, a feather and a hammer fall together, because there is no air.
explanations.art: A space capsule returning to Earth with a glowing heat shield, a trail of hot air behind it, and a small streak of a shooting star in the sky.

agreed.text: Drag pushes against the direction of motion, and gets bigger with speed, with the size facing the air, and with a blunt shape.
agreed.evidence: Wind tunnel tests on thousands of shapes, from planes to cyclists, give the same pattern.

agreed.text: A falling thing stops speeding up when its drag equals its weight.
agreed.evidence: Measured speeds of raindrops, parachutists and dropped balls level off at a steady value.

agreed.text: A streamlined shape has far less drag than a blunt shape of the same width.
agreed.evidence: In wind tunnels, a teardrop has more than ten times less drag than a flat disc of the same width.

agreed.text: Air gets thinner with height, so both drag and lift get smaller.
agreed.evidence: Weather balloons and aircraft instruments show the air density falling steadily with height.

agreed.text: Planes turn mainly by banking, which they do by changing the lift on parts of the wings and tail.
agreed.evidence: Pilots and flight recorders show that every turn begins with a roll of the wings.

agreed.text: Some birds that fly in a line save energy by catching the upwash of the bird ahead.
agreed.evidence: Tracking of ibises in 2014 showed each bird flapping in step with the one ahead, and a 2001 study found slower heartbeats in pelicans flying in a line.

challenging.claim: Heavy things fall faster than light things.
challenging.who: Aristotle taught this, and many people still think so.
challenging.for: In air a stone does fall faster than a feather.
challenging.against: Galileo argued in the early 1600s that without air, all things fall together. On the Moon in 1971, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather and they landed together. In air, drag makes the difference, not weight alone.

challenging.claim: Air is empty space, so a moving thing meets nothing.
challenging.for: You cannot see air, and it feels like nothing when you stand still.
challenging.against: A card swished through still smoke leaves whirls that keep turning. Air has weight, pushes back, and keeps moving after the thing has gone by.

challenging.claim: The most streamlined shape has a sharp, pointed front.
challenging.who: Many people, because arrows and rockets have pointed noses.
challenging.for: Pointed noses are used by arrows, rockets and fast jets.
challenging.against: At everyday speeds, the best shape is rounded at the front and tapered at the back, like a teardrop. A pointed nose helps mostly near the speed of sound or faster.

challenging.claim: Birds fly in a V only to see each other and follow the leader.
challenging.for: Birds in a V can see each other well.
challenging.against: Tracking showed that ibises place their wings to catch the upwash of the bird ahead and flap in step. Seeing probably matters too, so scientists still argue about how much of each.

challenging.claim: A plane turns by pointing its rudder, like a boat.
challenging.for: A plane has a rudder and a boat turns with one.
challenging.against: A plane mostly turns by banking. It rolls its wings over, and the lift then pulls it round the curve. The rudder only fine-tunes the turn.

big_questions.q: A raindrop falls a kilometre but lands slowly. Where did the energy of its fall go?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the drop had to push out of the way, all the way down.

big_questions.q: Is the air a bird flies in the same air that we walk in?
big_questions.hint: A hawk feels rising and sinking currents. A tiny wasp feels thick air. We feel almost nothing. Whose air is the real one?

big_questions.q: A plane that is easy to steer is hard to keep steady, and one that is steady is hard to steer. What should a pilot want? What should a bird want?
big_questions.hint: Think about a bird that needs to dodge a hawk, and a plane that carries 200 sleeping passengers.

big_questions.q: Geese take turns at the front of the V. Is this sharing, or does each bird look after herself?
big_questions.hint: Think about who works hardest at the front, and what the others gain.

big_questions.q: After a big plane has taken off, other planes must wait a few minutes before they use the same runway. What are they waiting for?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the plane leaves behind in the air.

big_questions.q: Small animals can fall from heights that would kill big ones. Does that mean small is better than big?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a small animal cannot do, as well as what she can.

big_questions.q: Sarla Thakral flew a plane alone in 1936, at the age of 21, and earned her pilot's licence, and she is often called India's first woman pilot. Why do some stories of flight get told more than others?
big_questions.hint: Think about whose names you were told, and whose you had to look up.

big_questions.q: When we say a bird uses the air, who is using whom? Could we say the air uses the bird?
big_questions.hint: Think about the whirls left behind, and who catches them.

story.title: The Wind's Shadow
story.note: A made-up story. The place is real: the quiet road from Vedaranyam towards Kodiyakarai (Point Calimere) in Tamil Nadu, where flamingos come in winter. The science is real. A rider close behind another rider feels less push from the air, because the front rider leaves a calmer patch of air behind her. Studies of cyclists find clearly less drag for the rider behind, with the size of the saving depending on how close the riders are. Riders in a line take turns at the front.
text: Thendral was the smallest girl in Class 4 at the panchayat school in Vedaranyam, and she had the oldest cycle. It had one speed, a squeaky bell, and a seat that her mother had lowered with a spanner that morning.

Every November, the school held a cycle rally to Kodiyakarai, where the flamingos come to the salt flats. The ride was twelve kilometres along a straight road, with open sky on both sides. The first team to reach the sanctuary gate would look through Mrs Selvarani's binoculars before anyone else.
Murugan, the tallest boy, looked at Thendral's cycle. 'The sea wind will blow you backwards,' he said. 'Girls at the back.'

Fathima, the strongest girl in the class, said nothing. She just tightened her scarf. Gomathi, who had a loud laugh, said, 'We will see.' The three girls made a team. The rule was that a team had to arrive together.
The boys shot off at the whistle. Fathima rode in front. Gomathi and Thendral followed.
By the second kilometre, the wind from the sea was pushing hard on Thendral's face. It whistled in her ears. Her legs began to ache. The boys were small shapes far ahead.
Then something odd happened. Thendral had been riding close behind Fathima's back, and she noticed the wind sounded different there. It had a hush in it. Her legs felt lighter.
She swung out to the side to look ahead. At once the wind slapped her cheeks so hard that her eyes watered. She tucked back in behind Fathima. The hush came back.
She did it again, to be sure. Out in the open, the wind pushed. Behind Fathima, it hardly did.
'Fathima Akka,' she called. 'Is it hard for you in front?'
'It is like pushing a wall,' Fathima panted.

Just then a line of flamingos crossed the road above them, pink and white against the blue. They flew one behind another, in a long slanting line. As Thendral watched, the front bird slid back to the end, and the next bird took her place.
'They take turns,' Thendral said, half to herself. Then she said it loudly. 'They take turns, because the one in front does the pushing!'
'What are you talking about?' said Gomathi.

'Fathima pushes the wind aside, and it leaves a quiet place behind her. We ride in her quiet. That is why it is easier back here. But she is working for all three of us.' Thendral took a breath. 'Let us each lead for two minutes. Then the front one drops to the back and rests.'
Fathima said, 'You are the smallest.'
'I will only lead for two minutes,' said Thendral. 'Then I will be in a quiet place again.'

So they tried it. Thendral went to the front. The wind hit her like a wet cloth, and she leaned over her handlebars and counted slowly to one hundred and twenty. Then she slid to the back, and the hush closed round her. Gomathi took the front, laughing. Then Fathima.
Soon they were passing the salt pans, with white heaps shining on both sides. The three girls rode in a neat line, and their legs kept turning.
At the eighth kilometre, they found Murugan sitting by the roadside with an empty bottle, breathing hard. He had ridden fast at the start, alone, and had pushed the whole wind by himself.
'How are you not tired?' he said.
Thendral stopped. 'Because the wind has a shadow,' she said. 'Behind a rider, the air is calmer. The front rider takes the hardest part. We take turns at the front.'
Murugan thought about this. 'Can I ride in your quiet?'
'Yes,' said Thendral. 'But you take your turn at the front.'
So four of them rode on together, and then Murugan took his turn, and then Thendral again. They reached the gate side by side, just as the first flamingos were landing on the shining water.
Mrs Selvarani held out the binoculars. 'Who wants the first look?'

Thendral looked at the others. Then she took the binoculars and found the line of birds. The front flamingo slid back to the end, and another took her place. Now Thendral knew exactly what they were doing.
story.epiphany: A moving body pushes the air aside and leaves calmer air behind it. A rider or bird that follows closely feels less push, so a line that takes turns at the front shares the work.
ask: Why was the wind quieter behind Fathima?
Why did the girls take turns at the front, instead of Fathima always leading?
If the wind blew from behind instead of from the front, would the quiet place behind a rider still help?

roots.context: We have raced parachutes, steered paper planes and watched smoke whirl behind a card. Now we ask what this tells us about the air, about flyers, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: After you swish a card through smoke, whirls of smoke keep turning where the card has been. A flyer moves the air they pass through, and that air keeps moving after the flyer has gone. In a flock, the next bird is held up by air the bird ahead has moved. So a flyer's push does not end at their wings.
deep_truth.habit: We picture air as empty space that a flyer passes through, and a flock as separate birds. But air is a real material that gets pushed. A flyer and the air around them work as one event.
deep_truth.evidence: In the smoke test, the whirls kept turning after the card had stopped. Northern bald ibises flying in a V were tracked in 2014, and each one flapped in step with the bird ahead to catch the air that bird had lifted.

three.who_am_i: When you walk across a room, you move the air as well as yourself. The air you push aside closes behind you, and your push goes on in it.
three.what_is_life: Flamingos and geese fly in lines and take turns at the front. Many living beings save effort by using what the others around them are already doing.
three.what_is_this_world: Nothing moves through the world without moving a little of it. The air a plane stirs is still moving minutes after the plane has gone.

roots.thread: A bird and the sky around her look like two things. But in the smoke test, a card and the air moved together, and the air kept the motion after the card stopped. A flock shares that motion from one bird to the next. Her muscles move her wings, her wings move the air, and the moving air lifts the next bird. In the end the motion becomes warmth in the air. The energy is not lost. It is only handed on.

teachings.source: Avatamsaka Sutra, the image of Indra's net
teachings.teaching: Imagine a net with a jewel at every knot. Each jewel shows the reflection of every other jewel. Nothing in the net stands alone.
teachings.link: Each flying bird's air reaches the next bird. A flock is a net of moving air, where each push is felt by the others.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at the hub of a wheel, but it is the empty space in the middle that makes the wheel useful. A cup is useful because of the space inside it.
teachings.link: The air looks like empty space. But the air is what a wing pushes on, and what lifts every flyer.

science.text: Northern bald ibises flying in a V were tracked in 2014 (Portugal and others, Nature). Each bird flapped in step with the bird ahead, to catch the rising air from that bird's wing tip.

Nobody can yet work out, from the basic equations, exactly how the swirling air behind a moving thing will behave. Whether those equations always have smooth answers is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven million-dollar prize problems.

other_view.view: A wake is only air moving according to the usual laws. Nothing is shared and nothing is used. To say a bird uses the air, or that the bird and the air are one event, is only a way of speaking, and it adds nothing to the sums.

practice.title: Feel the air go on moving
practice.say: Sit still and hold a card 20 centimetres from your cheek. Wave it towards your cheek once, slowly. Feel the puff arrive. Breathe in slowly. Now breathe out onto your palm and feel your own air moving. Think about where that air goes next.
practice.kid: Hold a card near your cheek. Wave it once. Feel the puff. Then breathe out on your hand. Feel the air move.

ask: When you walk across a room, do you move through the air, or do you move the air?
If a bird's push goes on in the air after she has passed, where does her flight end?
Is the air a hawk flies in the same air that you walk in?
roots.art: A card swished through a ribbon of incense smoke, with spiral whirls of smoke curling behind it, and a line of flamingos flying in the background.

games.title: Fix the Flyer: what is wrong, and what puts it right?
games.context: This is a guessing game about flying things. Each card shows a flyer with a problem, and three choices. You pick one and say why.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile on a table, and three tokens marked A, B and C in front of each player.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the other players each put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks A, B or C.

setup.art: Tokens turned over together and the reader showing the back of the card with the answer and the reason.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over. The reader shows the back.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a flyer with a problem and three choices on the front, and the answer with its reason on the back

items.f: A paper plane dives nose-first into the floor. A: Add a clip to its nose. B: Move the clip back towards the tail. C: Make the wings smaller.
items.b: B. The balance point is too far forward, so the nose is too heavy. Moving weight back levels the plane.

items.f: A paper plane climbs steeply, stops in the air and then swoops down. A: Bend the back edges of the wings up. B: Bend the back edges of the wings down a little. C: Add a clip to the tail.
items.b: B. The nose is rising too much. Bending the back edges down pushes the tail up, and the nose comes down.

items.f: A paper plane keeps turning left in a circle. A: Bend the back edge of its left wing down a little. B: Bend the back edge of its left wing up. C: Throw it harder.
items.b: A. The left wing is lifting less, so it drops and the plane banks left. Bending the left flap down gives that wing more lift.

items.f: A kite twirls and dives in the wind. A: Add a longer tail. B: Cut the tail off. C: Use a heavier string.
items.b: A. A tail adds drag at the back. This keeps the kite pointing the right way, in the same way as an arrow's feathers.

items.f: A shuttlecock is hit so that it flies feathers-first. What happens? A: It flips round and flies cork-first. B: It flies feathers-first all the way. C: It drops straight down.
items.b: A. The feathers have much more drag than the heavy cork. The drag swings them round behind the cork.

items.f: A small parachute and a big parachute carry the same coin and are dropped together. A: The small one lands first. B: The big one lands first. C: They land together.
items.b: A. The big canopy has more drag, so the air balances the weight at a lower speed.

items.f: The same parachute is dropped with 1 coin and then with 4 coins. A: The 1-coin one is faster. B: The 4-coin one is faster, but not four times faster. C: They land together.
items.b: B. A heavier load needs more drag to balance it, so the parachute falls faster. But four times the weight gives only about twice the speed.

items.f: You cycle into the same wind at 10, then at 20 kilometres an hour. How does the push of the air change? A: It stays the same. B: It doubles. C: It gets about four times bigger.
items.b: C. Twice the speed means twice as much air each second, hit twice as hard. Two times two is four.

items.f: A big raindrop falls from a cloud a kilometre up. How fast does it land? A: Faster than a bullet. B: About 30 kilometres an hour at most. C: It hardly moves.
items.b: B. Drag grows with speed until it equals the drop's weight, and then the drop stops speeding up.

items.f: Which of these shapes has the least drag in air? A: A flat plate facing the wind. B: A ball. C: A teardrop with the round end in front.
items.b: C. A teardrop lets air flow smoothly round it and close up behind, with a small wake.

items.f: Why do jets cruise about 10 kilometres up? A: The air is thin, so drag is less. B: They are nearer to the stars. C: There is no gravity there.
items.b: A. At 10 kilometres the air is about a third as dense, so there is much less drag and the jet burns less fuel.

items.f: On the Moon, an astronaut drops a hammer and a feather together. What happens? A: The hammer lands first. B: They land together. C: The feather lands first.
items.b: B. The Moon has no air, so there is no drag. Astronaut David Scott showed this on Apollo 15 in 1971.

items.f: Why can an ant fall off a table and walk away? A: Ants have very strong bones. B: A tiny body has a lot of skin for its weight, so drag slows her fall. C: Gravity pulls less on ants.
items.b: B. The smaller the animal, the more skin she has for her weight. Air slows her fall much more than it slows a bigger animal.

items.f: A bird in a V flies just behind and a little to one side of the bird ahead. Why there? A: To catch air rising near the wing tip of the bird ahead. B: To be hidden from hawks. C: There is no reason.
items.b: A. Measurements of ibises show this. Scientists also think the V helps birds see each other, and still argue about how much each one matters.

items.f: A plane banks to the left. Where does it turn? A: To the left. B: To the right. C: It goes straight on.
items.b: A. Banking tilts the lift sideways, and the sideways part of the lift pulls the plane round a curve to the left.

items.f: A pilot tips the elevator up. What does the nose do? A: It goes up. B: It goes down. C: It swings left.
items.b: A. The elevator up pushes the tail down, so the nose rises.

items.f: A paper plane has both back wing edges bent up. What does its nose do? A: It rises. B: It dips. C: Nothing changes.
items.b: A. Bent-up edges push the back of the wings down, and the nose tips up.

items.f: You swish a card through still smoke and stop. What does the smoke do? A: It stops at once. B: It keeps swirling for a moment. C: It is sucked towards the card.
items.b: B. The card moved the air, and the moving air carries on after the card has stopped.

items.f: Two cyclists ride in a line into a headwind. Who has the easier job? A: The one in front. B: The one behind. C: Both the same.
items.b: B. The front rider pushes the air aside and leaves calmer air behind her. The rider behind feels less push.

items.f: One paper cup faces the wind with its open side, and another shows its rounded back. Which feels the bigger push? A: The open side. B: The rounded back. C: Both the same.
items.b: A. The open cup catches the air, so it has more drag. This is why cup anemometers spin.

items.f: A skydiver wants to fall faster. A: Spread out her arms and legs. B: Tuck in her arms and legs, head-down. C: Open a bigger parachute.
items.b: B. A smaller body facing the air has less drag, so she must fall faster before drag balances her weight.

items.f: A paper plane has its balance point too far back. What happens? A: The nose rises and the plane stalls. B: The nose dives. C: It flies perfectly.
items.b: A. With too little weight at the front, the nose rises and the plane stops flying. It then drops.

items.f: A big plane has just taken off. Why must the next plane wait a few minutes? A: Swirling air left behind can toss a small plane. B: The runway needs cooling. C: The pilot needs a rest.
items.b: A. A big plane leaves strong whirls of air behind its wing tips. They keep moving long after the plane has gone.

items.f: Japan's 500 Series bullet train has a nose shaped like which bird's beak? A: A kingfisher. B: A crow. C: A peacock.
items.b: A. The nose was shaped to move through air smoothly, the way a kingfisher dives into water.

printables.title: 12 tokens: four marked A, four marked B and four marked C

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader keeps the back hidden.
Every other player puts one token face down for the choice they think is best. Then everyone turns the tokens over together.
The reader reads the back. A player whose letter matches the answer scores one point.
A player who also gives the right reason, using words such as drag, balance point, lift or thin air, scores one more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
After each card, the reader's job passes to the player on the left. With two players, the parent and child swap each card.
If you play alone, read the front, say your choice and your reason out loud, then turn the card over. Score yourself one point for each right choice. Try to beat your score next time.
The game ends when all 24 cards have been read. The player with the most points wins, and ties share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 12 tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player an A, a B and a C token.
flow.say: Each card shows a flyer with a problem. There are three choices, A, B and C. We pick one and say why.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take an A, a B and a C.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fix the Flyer. You set up the cards and the tokens.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card four, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Choose a token and turn it over together. Then the reader reads the back. Who can say why?
flow.kid: Read a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the fixes have in common?
good: They change how much the air pushes.
They change the lift or drag on one part.

flow.context: In this step, you play the first eight cards and learn how the scoring works.

flow.do: Play the next eight cards. Swap the reader after every card. Keep score on paper.
flow.say: Keep going. Think about drag, weight and the balance point. What would you change to put it right?
flow.kid: Play on. Think about drag, weight and the balance point.

ask.q: Which card surprised you so far, and why?
good: The hammer and feather land together on the Moon.
Four times the weight is only twice the speed.
The ant falls and walks away.

flow.context: In this step, you play the middle of the game and keep score.

flow.do: Play the last eight cards. When the pile is finished, count each player's points.
flow.say: Last cards. Think about what the air does to each flyer.
flow.kid: Play the last cards. Count your points.
flow.context: In this step, you finish the pile of cards and count the points.

flow.do: Say who won. Ask your child which card was hardest, and why.
flow.say: Who got the most points? Which card was hardest? What made it hard?
flow.kid: Who won? Which card was hardest? Why?
flow.think: Which fix would you try first on a real paper plane?
flow.context: This is the last step of Fix the Flyer. You look back at the game.

games.title: Pilot Says: pitch, roll and yaw with your body
games.context: This is an acting game like Simon Says. The leader gives flying commands, and the other players move their bodies like a plane.

setup.art: A child standing with arms out like wings in the middle of a clear room, with a parent holding a card.
setup.caption: 1. Clear a space. Everyone stands with arms out like wings.

setup.art: A leader reading a command card, with the other players tipping to one side with their arms.
setup.caption: 2. The leader reads a command. If it starts with Pilot says, everyone does it.

setup.art: A child standing still while the others move, and the leader pointing at her with a smile.
setup.caption: 3. A player who moves without the words Pilot says is out for that round.

printables.title: 16 two-sided cards: a command on the front, and what the real plane does on the back

items.f: Pilot says: Nose up! (Lean back a little, arms stay out.)
items.b: Pitch up. The elevator goes up, the tail is pushed down and the nose rises.

items.f: Pilot says: Nose down! (Lean forward a little.)
items.b: Pitch down. The elevator goes down, the tail is pushed up and the nose dips.

items.f: Pilot says: Roll left! (Tip your left arm down and your right arm up.)
items.b: Roll left. The left aileron goes up and the left wing lifts less, so it goes down.

items.f: Pilot says: Roll right! (Tip your right arm down.)
items.b: Roll right. The right aileron goes up and the right wing lifts less, so it goes down.

items.f: Pilot says: Yaw left! (Keep your arms level and turn your nose to the left.)
items.b: Yaw left. The rudder swings, and the nose points left without the wings tilting.

items.f: Pilot says: Yaw right! (Keep your arms level and turn to the right.)
items.b: Yaw right. The rudder swings the other way.

items.f: Pilot says: Bank left and turn! (Tip your left arm down and walk a small circle to the left.)
items.b: A banked plane turns because the lift tilts sideways and pulls it round the curve.

items.f: Pilot says: Bank right and turn! (Tip your right arm down and walk a small circle to the right.)
items.b: A plane banks right before it turns right, just as a cyclist leans before a bend.

items.f: Pilot says: Level out! (Arms flat, back straight, stand tall.)
items.b: In level flight, lift equals weight and thrust equals drag, so the plane flies straight and steady.

items.f: Pilot says: Dive! (Crouch down and lean forward.)
items.b: In a dive, the plane speeds up fast and the drag rises with the speed.

items.f: Pilot says: Climb! (Rise up on tiptoes with arms tilted up.)
items.b: A climbing plane needs extra thrust to beat both drag and the pull of gravity.

items.f: Pilot says: Spread your tail! (Spread your fingers wide behind you.)
items.b: A landing bird spreads her tail wide. It adds drag, which slows her, and helps her steer.

items.f: Pilot says: Stall! (Freeze with your arms up, then slowly crouch.)
items.b: In a stall the wing is tilted so far that the air cannot follow it. Lift drops away and the plane falls.

items.f: Pilot says: Fly in a V! (Line up behind a friend, a little to one side.)
items.b: Birds in a V catch the rising air from the wing tip of the bird ahead.

items.f: Pilot says: Change the leader! (The front player goes to the back.)
items.b: The front bird works hardest. Birds in a line take turns at the front.

items.f: Pilot says: Land! (Slowly lower your arms and crouch down.)
items.b: A landing plane slows down and loses height, and its flaps and wheels come out to add lift and drag.

rules: One player is the pilot and gives the commands. The pilot reads the front of a card aloud.
If the command starts with the words Pilot says, everyone does the move at once. If it does not start with those words, everyone stays still.
A player who moves when the pilot did not say Pilot says is out for one round, but can still play the next.
After each command, the pilot reads the back of the card. Everyone says what the real plane does.
The pilot's job passes to the next player after four cards. Play all 16 cards, or as many as you like.
Everyone who stays in is a good pilot. No one wins, but you can keep a count of the rounds you were never out.

flow.do: Cut out the 16 cards. Clear a space in the room, away from furniture and fans. Show your child how to hold their arms out like wings.
flow.say: We are going to be planes. Hold your arms out like wings. I will say a flying command, and you move like a plane.
flow.kid: Stand with your arms out like wings. You are a plane.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pilot Says. You clear a space and stand ready.

flow.do: Read the first six cards, in order. Read the front, let your child act, then read the back and ask the question below.
flow.say: Pilot says, nose up! Now tell me. What is the elevator doing on a real plane?
flow.kid: Do each move. Then listen to what the real plane does.

ask.q: What is different between a roll and a yaw?
good: In a roll, the wings tip.
In a yaw, the nose swings but the wings stay level.
A roll tips the wings and a yaw turns the nose.

flow.context: In this step, you learn the six moves of pitch, roll and yaw.

flow.do: Mix the next cards. Sometimes leave out the words Pilot says, to catch your child moving. Then swap roles.
flow.say: Now listen carefully. Only move if I say the magic words. Then you give me the commands.
flow.kid: Listen for the words Pilot says. Then be the pilot yourself.
flow.context: In this step, you play the full game, and then swap who is the pilot.

flow.do: Ask your child which move was hardest, and which one a bird could do easily.
flow.say: Which move was hardest to do? Which one do you think a crow does most?
flow.kid: Which move was hardest? Which does a crow do most?
flow.think: Why does a bird need to roll and yaw so easily?
flow.context: This is the last step of Pilot Says. You look back at the game.

experiments.title: Parachute Races: what slows a fall?
experiments.question: Does a bigger parachute fall more slowly? And does a heavier load make it fall faster, or four times as fast?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which will land first: a small parachute or a big one with the same coin? Will a parachute with 4 coins fall 4 times as fast as one with 1 coin? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every parachute is made from the same polythene, the same four strings and the same coins. Each is dropped from the same height, by the same person, in the same still room. Only one thing changes at a time: the size of the canopy, or the number of coins. Each is dropped three times and the times are averaged, because one drop can be spoilt by a gust or a tangle. The scrunched-up sheet is the control. It shows what the same polythene does with no canopy.

materials.item: a thin polythene carry bag or any light plastic sheet (a kirana bag is fine), to cut four squares from: one 20 centimetres wide and three 40 centimetres wide. A bag with no printing or creases works best
thread or thin string, cut into 12 pieces each 30 centimetres long
7 identical coins, such as one-rupee coins (about 4 grams each), or 7 small nuts or washers of the same size. Coins are small parts: keep them away from children under five
sticky tape and a pair of scissors
a ruler, and a phone or clock with a stopwatch (a phone in slow-motion video also works well)

masking tape or a sticky note, to mark a drop height of about 2 metres. The top of an ordinary room door is about 2 metres, so you can drop from there with no tape measure; or measure 2 metres once with a tailor's tape or string
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up holds each parachute at the 2 metre mark and does all the dropping from a steady floor. Nobody climbs on a chair. Coins are small parts: keep them away from children under five.
experiments.record: Write the three fall times for each parachute. Add the three times and divide by 3 to get the average. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each parachute, using the averages.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you make parachutes of two sizes, drop them with different loads, and time how long each takes to fall about 2 metres.

setup.art: Two squares of polythene on a table, a small one 20 centimetres wide and a big one 40 centimetres wide, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a small square (20 centimetres) and a big square (40 centimetres) from the bag.

setup.art: A square with a string taped to each corner, the four strings gathered in a knot, and a coin taped to the knot.
setup.caption: 2. Tape a string to each corner. Tape the four strings to a coin.

setup.art: An adult holding a parachute and coin at a tape mark on a wall about 2 metres up, and a child with a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 3. An adult holds a parachute at the 2 metre mark. The child gets the stopwatch ready.

setup.art: The parachute floating down with its canopy open, and the child starting and stopping the stopwatch.
setup.caption: 4. The adult lets go, and the child times the fall to the floor.

flow.do: Show your child the polythene, the strings and the coins. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will make parachutes. Which do you think will land first, a small one or a big one? And will 4 coins fall 4 times as fast as 1 coin? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We make parachutes. Which lands first, a small or a big one? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the big parachute will fall more slowly?
good: It is bigger, so the air pushes on it more.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guess for 4 coins as a number, such as '4 times as fast' or 'twice as fast'.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Parachute Races. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Cut a 20 centimetre square and a 40 centimetre square from the polythene. Tape a 30 centimetre string to each corner. Tape the four strings to one coin, so the strings are even.
flow.say: Cut the squares with a ruler. Tape one string to each corner. Gather the four loose ends and tape them to a coin.
flow.kid: Cut two squares. Tape a string to each corner. Tape the strings to a coin.
flow.parent: Make the squares exact. Make a third parachute with the big square and 4 coins taped together. Keep the strings even, or the canopy will lean. With 2 to 4 children, each child makes one parachute (A, B, C or D) and the same child does the dropping or timing for it, so all four are built at once. Label them A (small, 1 coin), B (big, 1 coin) and C (big, 4 coins). For D, scrunch the big sheet into a tight ball and tape it round 1 coin.

check.q: Why must the strings and the polythene be the same for every parachute?
options: So only the size or the load changes
So the parachutes look neat
So the polythene does not tear
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the strings or the sheet were different, you would not know what caused the difference in the fall.

flow.context: In this step, you make four things to drop: three parachutes and a scrunched control.

flow.do: Mark a spot about 2 metres up a wall with tape. Stand the adult underneath it. Hold parachutes A and B at the mark, one in each hand. Let go at the same moment and watch which lands first.
flow.say: Hold both at the same height. Let go together. Which lands first? Is it what you thought?
flow.kid: Hold two parachutes up high. Let go together. Which lands first?

ask.q: Both carry the same coin. Why does one land later?
good: The big one catches more air.
The big one has more drag.
The air pushes harder on the big canopy.

flow.parent: Hold each parachute by the middle of the canopy and the coin, then let go together. If a parachute folds up and drops like a stone, count it as a failed drop and do it again. Choose a room with the fans off and windows shut, because a breath of air spoils a parachute that falls slowly. Do not explain yet. Let your child say what they see.
flow.context: In this step, you race the small and the big parachute without a stopwatch.

flow.do: Time each of A, B, C and D three times. The adult drops from the mark. The child starts the stopwatch at the drop and stops it at the landing. Write each time in the table.
flow.say: Start the stopwatch as I let go. Stop it when it touches the floor. Write the time. We do each one three times.
flow.kid: Start the stopwatch at the drop. Stop it at the floor. Write the time.

ask.q: What happens to the fall time as the load gets heavier?

flow.parent: Typical times from 2 metres are about 2 seconds for the small parachute, about 3 to 4 for the big one, about 2 for the big one with 4 coins and under 1 second for the scrunched ball. Your numbers will differ, so trust your own table. The big parachute is the slowest and the scrunched ball the fastest; those two should be clear. The same person should use the stopwatch each time, because reaction time adds about a fifth of a second of error. Mark the time as a failed drop if the canopy folds, and drop it again. With several children, one drops, one times and one writes, and everyone swaps after each parachute. If the times are all too short to tell apart, ask a grown-up to drop from the top of a stair flight with a clear floor below.

check.q: Parachute B takes 2.8, 2.6 and 2.7 seconds. What is the average?
options: 2.7 seconds
2.6 seconds
8.1 seconds
check.why: Add the three times: 2.8 plus 2.6 plus 2.7 is 8.1. Divide by 3 to get 2.7. The sum, 8.1, is not an average.

flow.context: In this step, you time each parachute three times and write the results.

flow.do: Work out each average. Draw a bar chart with a bar for each of A, B, C and D. Compare C with A.
flow.say: Add the three times for each one, and divide by 3. Draw a bar for each parachute. Now look at C and A. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Find each average. Draw a bar for each one. Compare C and A.

ask.q: Does the parachute with 4 coins fall 4 times as fast as the one with 1 coin?
good: No, it is faster but not 4 times.
The time only got a bit shorter.

flow.parent: The big parachute with 1 coin (B) usually takes about twice as long as the same parachute with 4 coins (C), not four times. This is because four times the weight gives only about twice the terminal speed. C and A (big and heavy, small and light) often land at similar times. If nothing seems to differ between parachutes, check that the strings are even and the canopy opens, then try again. A big canopy with a heavy load can fall as fast as a small canopy with a light one.
flow.context: In this step, you work out the averages and draw the chart.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain terminal speed, once they have said their ideas.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: Why did the scrunched sheet fall so fast, when it is the same polythene?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the big canopy catches more air, so the air pushes back harder, and the parachute stops speeding up at a lower speed. After they have said what they saw, explain: a falling thing speeds up until drag equals weight. A bigger canopy gives more drag at the same speed, so the balance comes at a lower speed. A heavier load needs more drag, so the balance comes at a higher speed.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Parachute Races. You explain what you found.

experiments.title: Steer a Paper Plane: which flap turns it which way?
experiments.question: If you bend the back edges of a paper plane's wings, can you steer it? Which bend makes it climb, which makes it dive and which makes it turn?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What will a plane do if you bend the back edges of both wings up? What will it do if you bend one up and one down? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You fold every plane the same way, from the same kind of paper, and throw each one at the same speed, level, from the same spot. Only the bends at the back of the wings change. Each plane is thrown three times, because one throw can be spoilt by a wobbly arm. The plane with no bends is the control. It shows how the plane flies with no steering.
results_table: Bends at the back of the wings
Where it lands (steps from the start, and left or right)
Turn left, turn right, climb or dive?

materials.item: 5 sheets of A4 paper, or old notebook pages
a ruler and a pencil
masking tape or chalk to mark a start line
a clear space about 6 metres long, such as a corridor, a terrace or a big room
the results table

experiments.safety: Throw only when nobody is in front of you, and never at a face. Keep the pointed nose away from eyes.
experiments.record: For each plane, write what the nose does, where it lands, and whether it turns. Draw the path of each plane from above, with the start line and the landing spot.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you fold a paper plane, bend the back edges of its wings in different ways, and watch how each bend changes the flight.

setup.art: An A4 sheet folded in half lengthways and opened, then the top corners folded in to the centre line.
setup.caption: 1. Fold the sheet in half and open it. Fold the top corners to the centre line.

setup.art: The slanted edges folded in to the centre again, then the whole plane folded in half and the wings folded down.
setup.caption: 2. Fold the slanted edges to the centre. Fold in half. Fold the wings down.

setup.art: The back edges of both wings bent up by one centimetre, with a ruler beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Bend the back 1 centimetre of each wing, up or down, depending on the test.

setup.art: A child throwing a plane level from a start line, with chalk marks on the floor showing where it lands.
setup.caption: 4. Throw each plane level from the same line. Mark where it lands.

flow.do: Show your child the paper and the ruler. Ask for a guess and a reason for each bend. Write the guesses on the results table.
flow.say: We will fold a paper plane and bend the back of its wings. What will happen if both are bent up? And if one is up and one is down? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We bend the back of the wings. What will the plane do? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think a bend at the back of a wing changes the flight?
good: It changes how the air pushes on the wing.
It pushes the air up or down.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Mark the left and right wing with a pencil L and R, as seen by the pilot looking forward.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Steer a Paper Plane test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Fold one plane with the steps in the pictures. Press every crease flat with your fingernail. Make four more planes exactly the same way. Mark L and R on each.
flow.say: Fold the paper in half and open it. Fold the top corners in to the middle line. Fold the slanted edges in again. Fold the plane in half. Fold the wings down.
flow.kid: Fold a plane. Make four the same. Mark L and R on the wings.
flow.parent: Fold carefully so the planes are the same; ordinary A4 or notebook paper works, and thick card does not. With 2 to 4 children, each child folds one plane and checks a friend's. A plane with crooked wings will turn on its own, which spoils the test. Fold the wings so they are level and equal.

check.q: Why must all five planes be folded the same way?
options: So only the bends change
So they look neat
So they fit in a row
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the planes were different, you would not know whether the bends or the folds caused the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you fold five identical planes.

flow.do: Stand behind the start line. Throw plane 1, with no bends, three times, level and gently. Write what it does and where it lands each time.
flow.say: Throw it level, like putting a ball on a shelf. Do it three times. Write where it lands and which way it curves, if it curves.
flow.kid: Throw the plane three times. Write where it lands.
flow.parent: Plane 1 is the control. If it already curves, bend the wings level again, and refold if needed. Use the same gentle throw each time, and let the same child throw every plane, because a different arm changes the result more than a bend does. Fans off and windows shut. Others stand behind the thrower, one marks the landing spot with chalk or a pencil and one writes.
flow.context: In this step, you throw the plane with no bends, to see how it flies by itself.

flow.do: Bend both back edges of plane 2 up, by 1 centimetre. Throw it three times. Then bend both edges of plane 3 down. Then bend only the left edge of plane 4 up and the right edge down. Then do the opposite on plane 5. Write each result.
flow.say: For plane 2, bend both back edges up. Throw it three times and watch the nose. Then plane 3, both down. Then plane 4, left up and right down. Then plane 5, the opposite.
flow.kid: Bend the wing edges as the table says. Throw each three times. Write what the plane does.

ask.q: What does the nose do when both back edges are bent up?
When the left edge is up and the right edge is down, which way does the plane turn?
good: It turns towards the up flap.

flow.parent: A common result: both edges up make the nose rise, so the plane climbs steeply, stalls and lands short. Both edges down make it dive and land early. With the left edge up and the right edge down, the left wing lifts less and drops, and the plane turns left. Yours may differ a little, since a hand throw is never exactly the same. Compare the typical landing of the three throws, not the best one, and measure the sideways distance from the straight line in steps or shoe-lengths. If a plane does something odd, check that your throw was level and as gentle as before, and bend the edges more (2 centimetres). If a bend seems to do nothing, it is too small or the paper is too stiff to hold it.

check.q: Plane 4 has its left back edge up and its right back edge down. Which way will it most likely turn?
options: To the left
To the right
It will fly straight
check.why: A flap bent up makes its wing lift less, so that wing drops. The left wing goes down, the plane banks left and turns left. A plane turns towards the wing with the flap up.

flow.context: In this step, you bend the wings in four different ways and see how each one steers.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then explain pitch, roll and banking, once they have said their ideas.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think each bend would do? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: How does a bird steer, when she has no flaps?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that a bend up makes that part of the wing lift less, and a bend down makes it lift more. After they have said what they saw, explain: both flaps up push the back of the plane down, so the nose rises. One flap up makes one wing lift less, so it drops and the plane rolls. A rolled plane lifts sideways too, and that pulls it round a curve. Real planes do the same with elevators and ailerons, and birds twist their wings and tail.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Steer a Paper Plane test. You explain what you found.

activities.title: The Card in the Fan: how hard does the wind push?

materials.item: a table fan or pedestal fan with its grill on (switch off its side-to-side swinging)
a piece of stiff card from a cereal box, 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres, a one-rupee coin and sticky tape
thread about 40 centimetres long
a ruler to lay on the floor
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Hang the card in the fan's wind four ways. Measure how far each way is blown. Compare the pushes.

activities.safety: A grown-up sets up the fan and turns it on. Keep fingers and hair away from the fan grill.
activities.record: A table with four rows: card flat to the wind, card edge-on, card bent into a cup with the open side facing the fan, and the cup with its rounded back facing the fan. In each row, write how far the card was blown sideways, in centimetres.
activities.context: In this activity, you hang a card in the wind of a fan and find out how its shape changes the push of the air.

setup.art: A square of card hanging from a thread taped to a shelf, in front of a table fan, with a ruler on the floor under it.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the card in front of the fan. Lay a ruler on the floor under it.

setup.art: The card blown sideways by the fan wind, flat face to the fan, with the ruler showing how far it moved.
setup.caption: 2. Turn the fan on low. Read how far the card is blown.

setup.art: The same card bent into a cup, shown open-side to the fan and round-back to the fan.
setup.caption: 3. Bend the card into a cup. Test it both ways.

flow.do: Tape a coin to the bottom edge of the card so it hangs steady. Tape the thread to the top of the card. Tape the other end of the thread to a shelf, 50 centimetres in front of the fan. Lay the ruler on the floor under the card, with zero under the thread.
flow.say: The card hangs by a thread in front of the fan. The ruler on the floor will show how far the wind blows it. Which way of holding the card do you think the wind will push hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Hang the card. Lay a ruler under it. Guess which way gets pushed most.

ask.q: Which way of holding the card do you think the wind will push hardest, and why?
good: Flat to the fan, because it faces the most air.
The cup, because it catches the air.

flow.parent: Put the fan on its lowest setting. Keep the card at the same distance each time. The card should swing a clear 10 to 30 centimetres when flat to the wind. If it flies almost level, add a second coin; if it hardly moves, move the card closer to the fan. Then keep it the same for every test. Switch off the fan's side-to-side swing.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the card and the fan, and make a guess.

flow.do: Turn on the fan, low. Wait 10 seconds for the card to settle. Read how far it is blown, flat to the fan. Then turn it edge-on. Then bend it into a cup, open side to the fan. Then turn the cup round. Write the four readings. Do each one three times and write the middle value. To make the cup, curl the card round a pen and tape the edges.
flow.say: Wait until the card stops swinging. Then read the ruler. Do the flat card, the edge-on card, the open cup and the rounded back of the cup. Write each reading.
flow.kid: Wait for the card to settle. Read the ruler. Test all four ways. Write each reading.

ask.q: Which way did the wind push the card hardest? Which way least?
good: Flat or the open cup the most.
The rounded back of the cup less than the open side.

flow.parent: The flat card and the open cup are blown about the same, and the cup's rounded back about a third as far. Edge-on is blown almost nothing. Your numbers will differ. The cup's rounded back is blown clearly less than the open cup, even if not exactly a third. With several children, one holds the ruler, one reads, one writes, and each child bends a cup of their own. The cup is bent from the same card, so only its shape changes.

check.q: The open cup is blown further than the rounded back of the same cup. What does this show?
options: Shape changes how hard the air pushes
The cup got heavier
The fan blew harder on one side
check.why: The card, the fan and the distance were the same. Only the shape was turned round. So the shape made the difference in drag. This is why cup anemometers spin.

flow.context: In this step, you test the card in four ways and read the ruler.

flow.do: Ask your child what they noticed. Compare the four readings. Ask where else they have felt the same difference.
flow.say: Which way got the most push? Which got the least? Where have you felt this before, when you ran or rode a cycle?
flow.kid: Which way got the most push? Which got the least?
flow.think: Why does an open umbrella pull so hard in the wind?
flow.context: This is the last step of The Card in the Fan. You think about what you found.

activities.title: Whirls Behind a Spoon: the wake in a tray

materials.item: a large steel plate or baking tray with a rim, with about 2 to 3 centimetres of water in it
a pinch of black pepper, or turmeric powder, to sprinkle on the water (a fine powder floats best)
a round steel spoon (the back of the bowl), and a flat ruler or butter knife
a towel for spills

schedule.what: Pull a spoon and a ruler through the pepper and watch the whirls behind each.

activities.safety: Keep pepper away from eyes and noses, and skip it if anyone is allergic to pepper or turmeric. Wipe up spilled water at once so nobody slips.
activities.record: Draw the pepper on the water behind the round spoon and behind the flat ruler. Say which one left the bigger whirls, and for how long they kept turning.
activities.context: In this activity, you pull two shapes through water covered with pepper, to see the wake that each one leaves behind.

setup.art: A tray of still water with a thin layer of black pepper floating on top.
setup.caption: 1. Sprinkle a pinch of pepper on the still water.

setup.art: The back of a round spoon being pulled slowly across the tray, with pepper curling into two spinning whirls behind it.
setup.caption: 2. Pull the back of the spoon across the tray. Stop and watch.

setup.art: A flat ruler pulled edge-first through the pepper, with only a thin line of swirl behind it.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the ruler edge-first the same way. Compare the whirls.

flow.do: Fill the tray with 2 centimetres of water. Wait until the water is still. Sprinkle a very thin layer of pepper over it. Ask your child to guess which shape will leave the bigger swirl behind it.
flow.say: We will pull two shapes through the water. One is round and one is a thin edge. Which do you think will leave the bigger whirl behind it? Why?
flow.kid: Pepper on still water. Which shape leaves the bigger swirl? Why?

ask.q: Which shape do you think leaves the bigger whirls, and why?
good: The round spoon, because it is wider.
The spoon, because the water cannot close behind it.
The ruler edge, because it is thin.

flow.parent: Wait until the water is still, or the whirls will be mixed with ripples. Use a very thin sprinkle of pepper. A thick layer will not move.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the tray and make a guess.

flow.do: Hold the round spoon with its back down, just under the surface. Pull it slowly across the tray, about 15 centimetres in 2 seconds. Stop, and watch for 5 seconds. Sprinkle a little fresh pepper and wait until the water is still again. Then do the same with the ruler, edge-first.
flow.say: Pull the spoon slowly through the water. Then stop and watch the pepper. Now try the flat ruler, edge first, at the same speed. What is different?
flow.kid: Pull the spoon slowly across. Stop and watch the pepper. Then try the ruler.

ask.q: What does the pepper do behind the spoon after it stops?
good: It curls round in two circles.

ask.q: Which shape left the bigger wake?
good: The spoon, because the ruler cuts through.

flow.parent: The round spoon usually leaves two whirls that keep turning for a few seconds after you stop. The ruler edge-first leaves very little. If you see nothing, use less pepper, make the water 3 centimetres deep, wait for still water, and pull faster, about 15 centimetres in 1 second. Count how many seconds the whirls keep turning and write it down for the spoon and the ruler. It may take a few tries and the whirls may be faint, but a round shape leaves a bigger mess than an edge. One child pulls, one watches, one counts seconds; a phone filming in slow-motion shows the whirls clearly. Water and air are both fluids, and the same kinds of whirls form in air.
flow.context: In this step, you pull each shape through the pepper and watch the wake.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they saw. Ask what the whirls tell us about the water, and what the same shapes would do in air.
flow.say: The spoon is gone, but the water is still moving. What does that tell us about water? What do you think happens to air behind a bus?
flow.kid: The spoon stopped. Why does the water keep moving?
flow.think: If the water behind the spoon keeps moving, what does it have that it did not have before?
flow.context: This is the last step of Whirls Behind a Spoon. You think about what the wake shows.

activities.title: Swish in the Smoke: what a card leaves in the air

materials.item: one incense stick (agarbatti) and a holder
a piece of stiff card about the size of a postcard
a room with the fans off and the windows and doors closed, or a large cardboard box laid on its side to shelter the smoke from draughts
a dark background, such as a dark cloth or the inside of the cardboard box behind the incense

schedule.what: Light one incense stick. Swish a card near the smoke and watch the whirls.

activities.safety: A grown-up lights the incense and keeps it away from paper and cloth. Skip this activity if anyone has asthma, an allergy to smoke or breathing trouble, and keep it short (under ten minutes of smoke), and use Whirls Behind a Spoon instead. When you finish, the grown-up puts the stick out in a bowl of water and opens a window.
activities.record: Draw the smoke line before the swish, and the whirls after it. Write how long the whirls kept turning.
activities.context: In this activity, you swish a card through a thin line of smoke and watch the air keep moving after the card has stopped.

setup.art: A single incense stick in a holder, with a thin straight ribbon of smoke rising in a still, dark room.
setup.caption: 1. Light one stick in a still room. Wait for a thin, straight ribbon of smoke.

setup.art: A hand moving a card quickly past the smoke ribbon at a distance of 20 centimetres.
setup.caption: 2. Swish the card past the smoke, 20 centimetres away. Then stop.

setup.art: Spirals of smoke curling where the card went by, with the card held still beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Watch the smoke curl and spin after the card has stopped.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the incense stick and puts it in the holder. Close the windows and turn off the fans. Wait until the smoke rises in a thin, straight ribbon. Ask your child what the card will do to the smoke.
flow.say: The smoke is rising in a thin line. If I swish this card past it, what do you think the smoke will do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A thin line of smoke. What will the card do to it?

ask.q: What do you think the smoke will do when the card swishes past, and why?
good: It will curl, because the card moves the air.
