flow.parent: The room must be still. Even a person walking past will bend the smoke. Wait a minute for it to settle.
flow.context: In this step, you set up the smoke and make a guess.

flow.do: Hold the card about 20 centimetres from the smoke. Swish it quickly towards the smoke, then stop. Watch the smoke for 5 seconds. Try again with a slower swish. Then try it with the card edge-on.
flow.say: Swish the card past the smoke, then hold it still. Watch the smoke for as long as you can. Does the smoke stop when the card stops?
flow.kid: Swish the card near the smoke. Stop. Watch the smoke. Does it keep moving?

ask.q: What does the smoke do after the card has stopped?
good: It carries on swirling for a moment.

ask.q: What did the card move, since it did not touch the smoke?

flow.parent: A quick swish about 20 centimetres from the smoke usually bends the ribbon into curls that turn for a second or two. A slower swish makes less. If nothing happens, swish faster or move a little closer. Do not blow on the smoke. If the ribbon still wobbles on its own, put the stick inside the box on its side. In damp weather the smoke is thicker and slower to curl; swish more slowly. With several children, one swishes, one counts seconds the whirls last and one draws; take turns.

check.q: The card stopped, but the smoke kept curling. What does that show?
options: The moving air carried on after the card stopped
The card was still pushing the smoke
The smoke moves by itself
check.why: The card pushed the air, and the air carried the motion on to the smoke after the card had stopped. A moving thing leaves moving air behind it.

flow.context: In this step, you swish the card and watch what happens to the smoke.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they saw and what it means for a bird or a plane. Open a window and let the smoke go.
flow.say: The card never touched the smoke, yet the smoke moved. What did the card move? What would a bird leave behind in the air?
flow.kid: What did the card move? What does a flying bird leave behind?
flow.think: If the moving air carries on after a bird has gone, who could use that air?
flow.context: This is the last step of Swish in the Smoke. You think about what a flyer leaves behind.

activities.title: Find the Balance Point: hang it and mark it

materials.item: a piece of card from a box, about 15 centimetres by 20 centimetres, cut into any lopsided shape
a sharp pencil, to make small holes in the card
a pencil taped to the table so it sticks out past the edge, to hang the card from, and some thread (no pin needed)
a nut, a washer or a key to hang on the thread
a ruler, and a second cardboard cut-out of a bird or a plane

schedule.what: Hang the shape from two holes. Mark the lines. Find where they cross. Check by balancing.

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the holes by pushing a sharp pencil point through the card, on a pad of old newspaper, never over a hand.
activities.record: Draw the shape and the two lines. Mark where they cross. Write whether the shape balanced on a pencil tip at that spot.
activities.context: In this activity, you find the balance point of a lopsided card and of a bird or plane cut-out, and test that point.

setup.art: A lopsided card shape hanging from a pin, with a thread and a nut hanging from the same pin down in front of the card.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the card from a hole. Let a thread with a nut hang beside it.

setup.art: A line drawn on the card along the hanging thread.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a line on the card along the thread.

setup.art: The same card hanging from a second hole, with a second line crossing the first, and the card then balanced on a pencil tip at the crossing point.
setup.caption: 3. Hang it from a second hole and draw a second line. The lines cross at the balance point.

flow.do: Cut a lopsided shape from the card. A grown-up makes three small holes near the edge. Ask your child to guess where the shape will balance.
flow.say: Here is a lopsided shape. If I put one finger under it, where do you think it will balance? Why?
flow.kid: Here is a lopsided shape. Where will it balance? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think the shape will balance, and why?
good: Where there is the same weight on both sides.

flow.parent: The balance point is usually not the middle of a lopsided shape. It is nearer to the heavier part.
flow.context: In this step, you cut a shape and make a guess.

flow.do: Hang the shape from the first hole on the pencil that sticks out of the table. The hole is a little wider than the pencil, so the shape swings freely. Hang a thread with a nut from the same pencil. When everything is still, draw a line on the card along the thread. Do the same with a second hole. Look where the two lines cross. Balance the card flat on a blunt pencil tip or a fingertip at that spot.
flow.say: Let the thread hang still. Draw along it. Now do the same from another hole. The balance point is where the two lines cross. Try balancing the card there.
flow.kid: Hang the card from a hole. Draw along the thread. Do it again from another hole.

ask.q: Where do the two lines cross, and what happens when you balance the card there?
good: They cross near the heavy part.
The card balances flat on the pencil.
It balances at the crossing point.

flow.parent: The thread always hangs straight down from the hole. The balance point lies on that line. Where two lines cross, there is only one spot. If the card does not balance, redraw the lines more carefully. A third hole gives a third line; if all three cross at the same spot you have measured it well. With several children, each cuts a different shape and a friend holds the thread still.

check.q: Why does the card balance at the point where the two lines cross?
options: The weight is the same all round that point
The pencil pushes up harder there
The card is thinner there
check.why: The balance point is the one spot where the weight on every side is equal, so the card does not tip. It lies on every hanging line, so it is where the lines cross.

flow.context: In this step, you hang the card from two holes and find the balance point.

flow.do: Now do the same for a cut-out of a bird or a plane. Find its balance point. Ask your child where the wings are, compared with that point.
flow.say: Do the same for the bird shape. Where is the balance point? Is it near the wings or near the tail?
flow.kid: Find the balance point of the bird shape. Is it near the wings?
flow.think: What do you think would happen if a plane's balance point was in the wrong place?
flow.context: This is the last step of Find the Balance Point. You find it for a bird or plane shape.

activities.title: Why a Shuttlecock Always Turns Round

materials.item: a badminton shuttlecock, or a tight ball of newspaper with a ring of 6 paper strips (about 25 centimetres long and 3 centimetres wide) taped on as a skirt, plus a second ball with no strips
a clear space about 5 metres long

schedule.what: Throw a shuttlecock feathers-first and watch it turn. Try it with fewer feathers.

activities.record: Draw the path of a shuttlecock thrown feathers-first. Mark the point where it turns round.
activities.context: In this activity, you throw a shuttlecock backwards and watch it turn itself round in the air.

setup.art: A child tossing a shuttlecock gently with its feathers pointing forward.
setup.caption: 1. Toss the shuttlecock gently with the feathers pointing forward.

setup.art: A curved arrow showing the shuttlecock turning round in the air, with the cork now leading.
setup.caption: 2. Watch it turn round in the air.

setup.art: A homemade shuttlecock with a paper ball head and a skirt of paper strips.
setup.caption: 3. Try a homemade one with a paper ball and a ring of paper strips.

flow.do: Hold the shuttlecock by the cork. Ask your child to guess what will happen if you toss it into the air with the feathers pointing forward.
flow.say: I will toss the shuttlecock with the feathers pointing forward. What do you think it will do? Why?
flow.kid: I toss it feathers-first. What will it do? Why?

ask.q: What do you think a shuttlecock will do when it is thrown feathers-first, and why?
good: The heavy end will go first.

flow.context: In this step, you make a guess before you throw.

flow.do: Toss the shuttlecock gently, about 2 metres, with the feathers forward. Watch it turn. Try six tosses, in different directions, and tally how many turned cork-first. Then try the homemade one with its strips, and a ball with no strips for comparison.
flow.say: Toss it with the feathers forward. Watch the air. Does it keep going feathers-first? Try six tosses.
flow.kid: Toss it feathers-first. Does it turn round? Try six tosses.

ask.q: Which end leads in the end, the cork or the feathers?
good: It turns round so the cork is in front.

flow.parent: The shuttlecock should turn within about a metre and fly cork-first almost every time. Toss low and away from people and glass. One child tosses, one tallies and one watches where it turns. The ball with no strips should tumble and not turn the same way; if the strips ball also tumbles, make the strips longer. The feathers have much more drag than the cork, and drag pulls them behind. If you use the homemade one, the paper strips should trail behind the paper ball.

check.q: Why does the shuttlecock end up with the cork in front?
options: The feathers have more drag, so they trail behind
The cork is attracted to the ground
The feathers are heavier than the cork
check.why: The feathers catch much more air than the cork, so the air drags them behind. This swings the shuttlecock round until the cork is in front, in the same way as a tail steadies a kite.

flow.context: In this step, you toss the shuttlecock six times and watch it turn.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they saw, and where else a tail at the back keeps something pointing the right way.
flow.say: What turned the shuttlecock round? Where else have you seen a tail or feathers at the back that keeps something straight?
flow.kid: What turned it round? Where else is there a tail at the back?
flow.think: What would happen to an arrow with no feathers?
flow.context: This is the last step of the shuttlecock activity. You think about tails.

activities.title: Hide in the Wind's Shadow

materials.item: a table fan
a thin strip of tissue paper or a light ribbon, 20 centimetres long, taped to a stick
a large piece of cardboard, at least 30 centimetres wide (or a thick book), stood upright in front of the fan with clay or a pile of books; a round bottle to compare
a ruler, and a strip of paper marked at 5, 10, 20 and 40 centimetres

schedule.what: Hold a ribbon at different distances behind a book in the fan wind, and find the place where it hangs still.

activities.safety: A grown-up sets up the fan. Keep fingers away from the fan grill.
activities.record: A table with the distance behind the book (5, 10, 20 and 40 centimetres) and what the ribbon does at each: flutters, hangs, or flaps wildly.
activities.context: In this activity, you find out how far behind a blunt shape the wind is calm, which is the wind's shadow.

setup.art: A fan blowing at a ribbon on a stick, which flutters straight out in the wind.
setup.caption: 1. First hold the ribbon in the open wind. See how it flutters.

setup.art: A thick book standing in front of the fan, with the ribbon held close behind it, hanging calm.
setup.caption: 2. Stand a book in front of the fan. Hold the ribbon right behind it.

setup.art: The ribbon being moved further and further behind the book, from 5 to 40 centimetres, flapping more as it gets further away.
setup.caption: 3. Move the ribbon back a little at a time. Write what it does at each distance.

flow.do: Stand the book upright in front of the fan, about 30 centimetres away. A grown-up turns on the fan, low. Ask your child to guess what the ribbon will do right behind the book.
flow.say: The book stands in the wind. What will the ribbon do if I hold it right behind the book? What if I move it further back? Why?
flow.kid: A book in the wind. What will the ribbon do behind it? Why?

ask.q: What do you think the ribbon will do behind the book, and why?
good: Hang still, because the book blocks the wind.
Flap about as the wind goes round.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the fan and the book, and make a guess.

flow.do: Hold the ribbon in the open wind first. Then hold it 5 centimetres behind the book. Move it back to 10, 20 and 40 centimetres. Write what the ribbon does at each place.
flow.say: First hold the ribbon in the open wind. Then hold it close behind the book. Move it back a little at a time. Where does it start to flap?
flow.kid: Hold the ribbon behind the book. Move it back. Where does it flap again?

ask.q: Where is the wind calm, and where does it come back?
good: Close behind the book it is calm.
Further back it starts to flap.
At about 20 to 40 centimetres, it comes back.

flow.parent: The ribbon should hang quite still close behind the book, then flutter and flap as you move it away, and in some places it will flap oddly, as the air swirls round the edges. Your distances will differ. Switch off the fan's side-to-side swing. If the ribbon flutters everywhere, use the bigger board and a lower fan speed. Then try a round bottle in place of the board: which leaves the longer calm patch? One child holds the ribbon, one measures with the paper strip, one writes. This calm patch is called the wake or wind's shadow.

check.q: A rider cycles close behind another rider in the wind. Why does she find it easier?
options: She is in the calmer air behind the first rider
The first rider pulls her forward with a rope
The wind stops blowing on her
check.why: Just as the ribbon hung still behind the book, the air is calmer behind the front rider. The rider behind feels less push from the air.

flow.context: In this step, you move the ribbon back behind the book and write what it does.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they found, and how the same idea helps cyclists and geese.
flow.say: What did the book do to the wind behind it? How could a cyclist use this? How could a goose?
flow.kid: What did the book do to the wind? How could a cyclist use that?
flow.think: What if the rider in front gets tired? What could the line do?
flow.context: This is the last step of Hide in the Wind's Shadow. You think about riders and birds.

activities.title: Flock Watch: lines, tails and tilts

materials.item: a window, balcony or terrace with a view of the sky
paper and a pencil, and a pair of binoculars if you have them

schedule.what: Watch crows, pigeons, kites or egrets for 20 minutes, and record lines, tails and tilts.

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun, with or without binoculars. Stay behind the railing on a balcony or terrace, with a grown-up present. Do not touch or feed wild birds, and wash your hands afterwards.
activities.record: A tally of birds that flew in a line, birds that spread their tails, and birds that tilted their wings to turn. Add a drawing of one bird turning.
activities.context: In this activity, you watch real birds near your home, and see how they use their tails and wings to steer and how they fly in lines.

setup.art: A child at a window with paper, a pencil and a pair of binoculars, watching crows on a wire and a kite circling high.
setup.caption: 1. Sit by a window or on a terrace with paper and a pencil.

setup.art: A pigeon landing with her tail spread wide and her wings tilted up.
setup.caption: 2. Watch for a bird landing. Look at her tail and her wings.

setup.art: A line of egrets flying across a sunset sky, one behind another.
setup.caption: 3. Look for birds flying in a line or a V. Who is in front?

flow.do: Choose a spot with a view of the sky, such as a window, a balcony or a terrace. Write the three things to look for: lines, spread tails and tilting wings.
flow.say: We are going to watch the birds. Look for three things. Birds flying in a line. Birds spreading their tails. Birds tilting their wings. Which do you think we will see most?
flow.kid: Watch the birds. Look for lines, spread tails and tilting wings.

ask.q: Which of the three do you think you will see most often, and why?
good: Tilting wings, because birds turn all the time.

flow.context: In this step, you choose a spot and make a guess.

flow.do: Watch for 15 minutes. Make a tally mark for each bird in a line. Make one for each spread tail, and one for each wing tilt. Draw one bird turning.
flow.say: Make a mark each time you see one of the three. Watch a bird landing. What does her tail do? What do her wings do?
flow.kid: Make a mark for each thing you see. Draw one bird turning.

ask.q: What does a bird do with her tail and wings when she lands?
good: She flaps hard to slow down.

flow.parent: Crows, pigeons, mynas and kites are usually easy to find, even in a city. In the evening, egrets and parakeets often fly in lines to their roosts. If no birds come, try again at dusk or in the early morning. A landing bird spreads her tail to add drag and slow down. A kite circling with tilted wings is the easiest to see. With several children, each takes one tally (lines, tails or tilts) and then you add them up.

check.q: A pigeon spreads her tail wide as she lands. Why?
options: The wide tail adds drag and slows her down
She wants to look bigger
She has to push the air up
check.why: A wide tail catches more air, so the drag is bigger and it slows her down. Birds also tilt the tail to steer, in the same way as the flaps on a plane.

flow.context: In this step, you watch the birds and make marks.

flow.do: Ask your child to share what they saw and which bird surprised them.
flow.say: What did you see most? Which bird did something you did not expect?
flow.kid: What did you see most? What surprised you?
flow.think: How is a bird's tail like the tail of a kite?
flow.context: This is the last step of Flock Watch. You share what you saw.

projects.title: Straw Hoop Glider: a plane with no wings

materials.item: a drinking straw, as wide as you can find (a juice or smoothie straw); a plain straw also works
an A4 sheet of paper, or a strip of thin card
sticky tape and a pair of scissors
a ruler and a pencil
a clear space about 6 metres long

schedule.what: Cut two paper strips. Make two hoops. Tape them to the straw. Fly it. Test some changes.

projects.safety: Use scissors carefully. Do not throw the glider near anyone's face. Stand all other children behind the thrower.
projects.record: Draw the glider with its two hoops. Write how far it flew with the small hoop in front. Write what happened when you changed one thing.
projects.context: In this project, you make a glider from a straw and two paper rings, which looks nothing like a plane but still flies.

setup.art: A paper sheet cut into two strips, one 3 centimetres by 15 centimetres and one 3 centimetres by 25 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Cut two strips: a short one and a long one.

setup.art: Each strip curled into a ring with the ends overlapping 1 centimetre, and taped.
setup.caption: 2. Curl each strip into a ring and tape the ends together.

setup.art: A straw with the small ring taped near the front end and the big ring taped near the back end.
setup.caption: 3. Tape the small ring to the front of the straw and the big ring to the back.

setup.art: A child throwing the glider gently, with the small ring leading.
setup.caption: 4. Hold the straw in the middle. Throw it gently, small ring first.

flow.do: Show your child the straw and the paper strips. Ask them to guess if a straw with two paper rings can fly, and why.
flow.say: This is a glider with no wings. It is a straw with two paper rings. Do you think it will fly? Why?
flow.kid: A straw with two rings. Will it fly? Why?

ask.q: Do you think a glider with no wings will fly, and why?
good: No, because it has no wings.
Yes, because the rings are like wings.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most children are surprised that it flies.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Straw Hoop Glider. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Cut one strip 3 centimetres by 15 centimetres and one 3 centimetres by 25 centimetres. Curl each into a ring, with the ends overlapping 1 centimetre, and tape them. Tape the small ring near the front end of the straw. Tape the big ring near the back end.
flow.say: Cut two strips, one short and one long. Curl each into a ring. Tape the small ring to the front of the straw. Tape the big ring to the back.
flow.kid: Cut two strips. Curl them into rings. Tape the small ring to the front.
flow.parent: The rings should be as round as you can make them. Tape the straw to the inside wall of each ring, so the rings are short tubes lying along the straw, like a hula hoop that is open front and back, not hanging from it.
flow.context: In this step, you make the glider.

flow.do: Hold the straw at its middle with the small ring in front. Throw it gently and level, like a dart. Throw it five times. Measure how far it flies on the best throw.
flow.say: Hold it in the middle. Throw it gently and level, with the small ring leading. Does it fly? How far?
flow.kid: Throw it gently, small ring first. How far does it fly?

ask.q: Why do you think a glider with no wings can fly?
good: The air pushes up on the rings.

flow.parent: A good throw is gentle and level, not hard and upward. It should glide a few metres. If it dives, move the front ring slightly back. If it stalls and drops, move the big ring a little further back. The rings work as round wings that push air down. If it still dives, tape a small ball of clay or a few pieces of tape to the straw's front. Measure the best throw in steps. Each child makes one glider and the group compares distances. Hold the straw at its middle and throw it level, not hard.

check.q: Why is it better to throw the hoop glider gently than hard?
options: A hard throw makes drag very large and the glider tumbles
A hard throw makes it too heavy
A gentle throw makes the air thicker
check.why: Drag grows very quickly with speed. A hard throw makes the drag very large, and a light glider is thrown off course. A gentle, level throw lets the glider find its steady glide.

flow.context: In this step, you throw the glider and measure how far it flies.

flow.do: Change one thing at a time and throw again. Turn the glider round so the big ring is in front. Tilt the small ring a little to one side. Then make the small ring smaller. Write what each change does.
flow.say: Change just one thing. First put the big ring in front. Then tilt the small ring a little. What does each change do?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Throw it again. What changes?

ask.q: What happens when the big ring is in front?
What happens when you tilt the small ring a little?
good: The glider turns to one side.

flow.parent: Most families find that with the big ring in front, the glider flies poorly or tumbles. Tilting a ring may make it turn, because the ring then pushes the air to one side. Write what you see, even if it is not what you expected.
flow.context: In this step, you change one thing at a time and see how it steers.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they saw and why. Ask which ring does the job of the tail.
flow.say: Why does it fly with the small ring in front? Which ring works like a tail?
flow.kid: Why does it fly with the small ring in front?
flow.think: Why is the big ring at the back like the feathers of a shuttlecock?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Straw Hoop Glider. You explain what you saw.

projects.title: A Cup Wind Meter: spin it and count

materials.item: 4 small paper cups, the same size (chai-stall cups are fine)
2 drinking straws and a stapler
a pin and a pencil with a rubber at the end
a marker pen, to colour one cup
a table fan with at least two speeds, and a phone or clock with a stopwatch

schedule.what: Build the cup wind meter. Test it in the wind of a fan at three settings. Count the turns.

projects.safety: A grown-up pushes the pin and helps with the stapler, and puts the pin and staples away after, because both are sharp and small. Keep fingers away from the fan grill.
projects.record: A table with the fan setting (low, medium, high) and the number of turns in 30 seconds. Draw a bar chart of the three results.
projects.context: In this project, you build a spinning cup wind meter like the one on a weather station, and use it to measure the wind of a fan.

setup.art: Two drinking straws crossed in the middle, held by a pin, with a cup stapled to the end of each straw.
setup.caption: 1. Cross two straws and pin them in the middle. Staple a cup to each end.

setup.art: The pin pushed into the rubber on top of a pencil, with the four cups all facing the same way round.
setup.caption: 2. Push the pin into the rubber of a pencil. All cups face the same way round.

setup.art: The cup meter spinning in front of a table fan, with one cup coloured to count the turns.
setup.caption: 3. Hold it in the wind of the fan. Count how many times the coloured cup goes round.

flow.do: Show your child a cup and the straws. Ask for a guess about which way the cups will spin, and why.
flow.say: We will make a wind meter, with four cups. Each cup has an open side and a rounded back. Which do you think the wind pushes harder? Why?
flow.kid: A cup has an open side and a rounded back. Which gets pushed more?

ask.q: Which part of the cup will the wind push harder, and why?
good: The open side, because it catches the air.
The open side has more air to push on.

flow.parent: Remind your child of the cup in the fan (The Card in the Fan activity), if they did it. Anna Mani, an Indian physicist from Kerala, led work on making wind and sunshine instruments for India's weather service.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cup Wind Meter. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Cross the two straws in the middle, and push a pin through both. Staple a cup to each end of each straw, so all four cups face the same way round. Push the pin into the rubber of the pencil. Blow gently to make sure it spins freely. Colour one cup with a marker.
flow.say: Cross the straws and push the pin through the middle. Staple a cup to each end. The open sides must all face the same way round. Push the pin into the pencil rubber, and blow to test it.
flow.kid: Cross the straws. Staple a cup at each end. All cups face the same way.
flow.parent: The cups must all face the same way round, such as every open side pointing clockwise, or the meter will not spin. The pin must be loose enough in the straws so the cups can turn. If it grinds, make the pin hole a little bigger.

check.q: Why must all four cups face the same way round?
options: So the wind pushes harder on the open sides than on the backs, and the cups keep turning
So the cups look neat
So the cups weigh the same
check.why: The open side of a cup has more drag than its rounded back. If all cups face the same way, the push is bigger on one side, and this difference keeps the meter turning. If they faced different ways, the pushes would cancel.

flow.context: In this step, you build the cup wind meter.

flow.do: A grown-up turns the fan on low. Hold the meter 50 centimetres in front of it. Count how many times the coloured cup goes round in 30 seconds. Write the number. Do the same on medium and high. If your fan has one speed, hold the meter at 100, 50 and 25 centimetres instead.
flow.say: Hold the meter in the wind. Count how many times the coloured cup goes round in 30 seconds. Write the number. Then try the next fan speed.
flow.kid: Hold the meter in the wind. Count the turns in 30 seconds. Write it down.

ask.q: What happens to the number of turns as the fan speed goes up?
good: The faster the wind, the more turns.

flow.parent: Hold it at the same distance each time. Your numbers will differ. A meter like this might make roughly 10 to 60 turns in 30 seconds, depending on your fan. If it spins too fast to count, count for 10 seconds and multiply by 3. The count shows which wind is stronger, not the speed in kilometres an hour. Each child can build a meter and the group can compare them. Count with a partner, one watching the cup and one watching the clock.
flow.context: In this step, you test the wind meter at three fan speeds.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart of the three results. Ask your child what the chart shows, and how a weather station might use a meter like this.
flow.say: What does the chart show? How could a weather station use a spinning wind meter?
flow.kid: What does your chart show? How is a weather station like this?
flow.think: How could you turn the number of turns into a wind speed in kilometres an hour?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Cup Wind Meter. You show your results.

challenges.title: Soft Landing: the slowest parachute
challenges.problem: Make a parachute that carries 2 coins and takes the longest time to fall about 2 metres. It must open, stay open, and land upright.
constraints: Use one thin polythene sheet, no bigger than 50 centimetres by 50 centimetres, and thread, tape and scissors only.
The load is 2 coins taped together. The parachute must carry both.
An adult drops it from the same 2 metre mark every time.
Time three drops and use the average.
materials: a thin polythene sheet from a carry bag
a pair of scissors and a ruler
general: A big square canopy with a string at each corner, like the Parachute Races.
A round canopy cut in a circle, which opens evenly.
Long strings so that the canopy opens fully before the load.
creative: A small hole in the middle of the canopy, called a vent, to stop it swaying from side to side.
A canopy in the shape of a bowl, with more strings so that the edge stays wide open.
Two canopies, one above the other, joined by the same strings.
challenges.your_turn: Draw your design. Build it and time three drops. Change one thing, such as the size of the canopy or the length of the strings, and time it again. Which design fell most slowly? Why do you think it did?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about drag and falling. You build the slowest parachute you can.

setup.art: A child sketching three parachute designs: a square, a circle and a bowl, each with a coin underneath.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some designs.

setup.art: A parachute with a round canopy and long strings being taped to two coins.
setup.caption: 2. Build your best design.

setup.art: An adult dropping the parachute from the 2 metre mark while a child times it.
setup.caption: 3. Drop it from 2 metres and time the fall.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Ask your child to sketch two or three designs and say which they expect to be slowest.
flow.say: We want the slowest fall. Which design will do best? What makes a parachute slow?
flow.kid: Sketch some designs. Which will fall most slowly?

ask.q: What makes a parachute fall slowly?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Soft Landing challenge. You think and sketch.

flow.do: Build your best design and test it. Time three drops from the 2 metre mark. Write each time and work out the average.
flow.say: Build your best design. Time it three times, and find the average.
flow.kid: Build your parachute. Time it three times.
flow.parent: If the canopy folds up and falls fast, it did not open. Try longer strings or a stiffer rim.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test the first design.

flow.do: Change one thing, such as the size of the canopy, a vent hole or the string length. Test it again. Choose the design with the longest average time.
flow.say: Change just one thing, and test again. Which design wins? Why?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test it. Which wins?
flow.think: Why would a hole in the middle of the canopy make it steadier, though it lets air through?
flow.context: In this step, you change one thing and find the best design.

challenges.title: Fly Straight, Then Fly Left: control a paper plane
challenges.problem: Make one paper plane that lands on a target mat 5 metres away, and then change the same plane so that it curves left to land on a mat 2 metres to the left.
constraints: Use one A4 sheet of paper, tape and up to two paper clips.
Throw from a fixed line. The target mat is a sheet of newspaper.
You may bend the back edges of the wings or move the clips, but you may not cut the plane.
Try each target five times and count how many land on the mat.
materials: newspaper sheets for the target mats
a clear space about 6 metres long
general: A dart plane with a clip on the nose to make it fly straight.
A small bend at the back of both wings to fine-tune the climb.
A smooth, level throw that stays the same each time.
creative: Bend only the left wing's back edge down a little, so that the plane turns right, then reverse it.
A paper tail fin made of a folded strip at the back.
Moving a paper clip to one wing tip to make the plane lean.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your plane and say where you will put the bends and clips. Fly it at the first target five times. Then change it to reach the second target. What did you change, and why did that steer the plane?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about stability and steering. You tune a paper plane to hit two targets.

setup.art: A paper plane next to two newspaper mats on the floor, one straight ahead 5 metres away and one 2 metres to the left.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the mats. Mark the start line.

setup.art: A child bending the back edge of one wing of a paper plane and adding a paper clip to the nose.
setup.caption: 2. Tune the plane with bends and clips.

setup.art: A plane landing on a mat, with a tally of hits written beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Fly it five times at each mat. Count the hits.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Ask your child to say what they will change to make a plane fly straight, and what to turn it left.
flow.say: What will you change to make it fly straight? What will you change to make it curve left? Why?
flow.kid: What makes a plane fly straight? What makes it turn left?

ask.q: What would you change to turn a plane left?
good: Bend the left wing's back edge up.
Make the left wing lift less.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Fly Straight, Then Fly Left challenge. You plan.

flow.do: Fold your plane. Tune it with bends and clips until it lands on the near mat. Fly it five times and count the hits.
flow.say: Fold your plane. Tune it with bends and clips. Fly it five times at the near mat. Count the hits.
flow.kid: Tune your plane. Fly it five times at the near mat.
flow.parent: If the plane dives, move a clip back. If it climbs and stalls, bend the back edges down a little. If it drifts, check the wings are equal.
flow.context: In this step, you tune the plane to fly straight.

flow.do: Change the plane so it curves left to the second mat. Fly it five times and count the hits. Write what you changed.
flow.say: Now make the plane curve left. Which flap will you bend? Fly it five times. Count the hits.
flow.kid: Make your plane turn left. Fly it five times. Count the hits.
flow.think: How did you know which wing to change?
flow.context: In this step, you change the plane so that it turns left.

items.p: Which sentence says what drag is?
opts: The push of air against a thing moving through it
The pull of the Earth on a falling thing
The push that makes a plane go forward
items.why: Drag is the air pushing back against anything that moves through it. The pull of the Earth is weight, and the push forward is thrust.

items.p: Drag always pushes ____ the direction the thing is moving.
a: against
opposite to
opposite
items.why: Drag pushes back against the motion. That is why it slows things down.

items.p: A card held edge-on to the wind feels the same push as the same card held flat to the wind.
items.why: False. The flat card faces much more air, so the push is much bigger. Edge-on, it hardly faces the air at all.

items.p: A cyclist rides into the wind at 10 kilometres an hour, and then at 20. About how much bigger is the push of the air at 20?
opts: About 4 times
About 2 times
The same
items.why: At twice the speed she meets twice as much air each second, and hits each bit twice as hard. Two times two is four.

items.p: Match each thing in the wind to how much drag it has.
pairs: An open umbrella facing the wind
a lot of drag
A closed umbrella pointing into the wind
little drag
A flat plate facing the wind
a lot of drag
A teardrop with its round end forward
very little drag
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Drag is big when a blunt shape faces the air, and small when the shape is streamlined or is turned edge-on.

items.p: Does each of these make the drag on a cyclist bigger or smaller?
items: Wearing a loose shirt that flaps
items.a: as given
items.why: A smaller, smoother body facing the air has less drag. Flapping cloth, sitting up and extra speed all add drag. A rider behind another rides in calmer air.

items.p: A raindrop falls at a steady 6 metres each second. How many metres does it fall in 10 seconds?
items.why: 6 metres each second for 10 seconds is 6 times 10, which is 60 metres.

items.p: A big raindrop stops speeding up as it falls. What does this tell you?
opts: The drag has grown as big as its weight
Gravity has stopped pulling it
The cloud stopped pushing it
items.why: When drag equals weight, the forces are balanced and the drop falls at a steady speed. Gravity is still pulling it.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for a parachute that you let go.
a: You let go and it starts to fall
It speeds up and the drag grows
The drag becomes as big as its weight
It falls at a steady speed
items.why: A falling parachute speeds up and the drag grows with its speed. When the drag equals the weight, it falls at a steady speed.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A parachute canopy, an open umbrella, a kingfisher's beak, a flat sheet of card.
items.a: The kingfisher's beak, because it is streamlined and cuts through air with little drag. The other three are wide and flat, with a lot of drag.
items.why: The beak is rounded at the front and tapers to the back, so air flows smoothly round it. The others are made to catch or block the air.

items.p: Draw a parachute falling at a steady speed. Draw an arrow for its weight and an arrow for the drag, and say how long each arrow is.
items.a: A parachute with a down arrow for weight and an up arrow for drag. Both arrows are the same length.
items.why: At a steady speed the forces are balanced, so the arrows are equal and opposite.

items.p: Two parachutes carry the same coin. The big one lands later than the small one. Explain why, using the word drag.
items.a: The big canopy catches more air, so it has more drag at the same speed. The drag equals the weight at a lower speed, so it falls more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer says that a bigger canopy has more drag, so the forces balance at a lower speed.

items.p: A parachute with four times the weight falls four times as fast.
items.why: False. A heavier load falls faster, but four times the weight gives only about twice the speed.

items.p: A badminton shuttlecock is hit sideways. Why does it end up flying cork-first?
opts: The feathers have more drag and trail behind the heavy cork
The cork pulls it towards the ground
The feathers are heavier than the cork
items.why: The feathers catch much more air than the cork, so the drag swings them behind. This steadies the shuttlecock.

items.p: Imagine a friend says: Heavy things always fall faster than light things.

views.says: Heavy things fall faster than light things, and that is what we see with a stone and a feather.

views.who: Galileo, an Italian scientist of the early 1600s
views.says: In air, the feather is slowed by drag. Without air, all things fall together.

views.who: An astronaut on the Moon in 1971
views.says: I dropped a hammer and a feather, and they landed at the same moment, because there is no air here.

items.ask: Whose view fits what you saw in the parachute races? What does drag do to the stone and the feather?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer says that in air, drag slows the light, wide feather more than the stone, and with no air they fall together.
items.why: In the parachute races, the big canopy fell slowly because of drag. Weight alone is not what sets how fast things fall in air.

items.p: Name two ways a cyclist can reduce the drag on herself, and say why each works.
items.a: She can crouch low, so less of her faces the air. She can wear a smooth, tight helmet and clothes, so the air flows round her and does not catch on flapping cloth.
items.why: Drag depends on the size of the area facing the air and on shape. Making herself smaller and smoother reduces both.

items.p: Why does a heavier parachute fall faster than a lighter one with the same canopy?
opts: It needs more drag to balance its weight, so it must go faster
Gravity pulls harder on heavy things in a different way
A heavier parachute has a smaller canopy
items.why: Drag grows with speed. A heavier load needs more drag to balance it, so the drag only grows enough at a higher speed.

items.p: Four times the weight gives only about ____ times the falling speed.
a: two
items.why: The speed grows with the square root of the weight. The square root of 4 is 2.

items.p: Match each part of a plane to what it does.
pairs: Elevator
tips the nose up or down (pitch)
Aileron
tilts the wings (roll)
Rudder
swings the nose left or right (yaw)
Propeller or engine
gives thrust to go forward
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each part changes one thing. The elevator pitches the plane, the ailerons roll it, the rudder yaws it, and the engine pushes it forward.

items.p: On a paper plane, what does each bend at the back of the wings do to the plane?
items: Left edge up and right edge down
Right edge up and left edge down
A raised elevator on a real plane
items.a: as given
items.why: Bends that match on both wings pitch the plane. Bends that are opposite roll it.

items.p: A plane mainly turns by banking, which tilts the lift sideways.
items.why: True. When the wings are tilted, part of the lift pulls the plane sideways, and it goes round a curve.

items.p: A car at 40 kilometres an hour has some amount of air drag. At 120 kilometres an hour, how many times bigger is that drag?
items.why: 120 is three times 40. The drag grows with the square of the speed, so it is 3 times 3, which is 9 times bigger.

items.p: Put these in order, for how a plane makes a left turn.
a: The pilot rolls the plane to the left
The wings tilt and the lift tilts sideways
The sideways part of the lift pulls the plane left
The plane flies round a curve to the left
items.why: A turn begins with a roll. The tilted lift then has a sideways part that pulls the plane round the curve.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? A shuttlecock's feathers, an arrow's feathers, a kite's tail, a flat stone.
items.a: The flat stone, because it has no tail. The other three are at the back and keep the thing pointing the right way.
items.why: Feathers and tails add drag at the back, which keeps the front pointing forward. A stone has no such part.

items.p: Draw a V of geese seen from above. Add small arrows to show where the air rises beside the wing tip of the goose in front.
items.a: A V shape with a goose at the front and others behind, each slightly to one side. Small upward arrows are drawn just outside the wing tip of each goose.
items.why: A bird behind and to one side can catch the rising air from the wing tip of the bird in front. This is called upwash.

items.p: A mouse can fall down a deep well and walk away, but a person would be badly hurt. Explain why, using the words skin and weight.
items.a: A mouse has a lot of skin for her weight, so air slows her fall far more. A person has less skin for their weight, so they fall much faster.
items.why: A strong answer says that a small body has more skin for its weight than a big one, so drag slows it more.

items.p: A jet lands at a much lower speed than it cruises. Why does it need to go faster when it flies high?
opts: The thin air gives less lift, so the wings must move faster
The engines are stronger at height
Gravity is stronger at height
items.why: Lift depends on how much air the wings push down. Thin air gives less lift at the same speed, so the plane must go faster to make enough.

items.p: In space, an aircraft's wing flaps could steer a spacecraft.
items.why: False. Flaps work only by pushing on air. With no air, they do nothing, so a spacecraft steers by firing small rockets.

items.p: Scientists argue about why birds fly in a V.

views.says: Birds put themselves where the air is rising behind the bird ahead, and flap in step. They save energy.

views.who: A scientist who studies how flocks stay together
views.says: A V lets every bird see the others. Seeing may matter as much as energy.
Perhaps it is both. A shape can do more than one job at the same time.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? What evidence would help you decide?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a view and says what could be measured, such as the birds' heart rates or their positions.
items.why: Scientists do not yet agree how much of the V is for saving energy and how much is for seeing. Tracking the birds' wing tips and heartbeats gives evidence.

items.p: Why must a paper plane have more weight near its nose than near its tail?
items.a: If the balance point is near the front, a bump makes forces that turn the nose back down to level. With too little weight at the front, the nose rises, the plane stalls and it falls.
items.why: A strong answer says that the balance point should be ahead of the centre of lift, so the plane tends to come back to level flight.

items.p: On an anemometer, all the cups face the same way round. Why does it spin?
opts: The wind pushes harder on the open sides than on the rounded backs
The cups are heavier on one side
The wind blows only on one cup
items.why: An open cup has more drag than its rounded back. The difference in push keeps the anemometer turning.

items.p: A spacecraft that comes back from space has a heat shield because drag turns its ____ into heat.
a: motion
speed
movement
items.why: The spacecraft hits the air at a great speed. The drag turns its motion into heat, and the shield takes it.

items.p: A bird spreads her tail wide as she lands. Explain what that does to the forces on her.
items.a: A wide tail catches more air, so the drag is bigger and she slows down. She can also tilt the tail to steer.
items.why: A spread tail adds drag, which slows her, and a tilted tail changes the air push on her back, which helps her turn.

items.p: In a test, parachute A (a small canopy and 1 coin) fell in 1.4 seconds. Parachute B (a big canopy and 1 coin) took 2.7 seconds. Parachute C (the big canopy and 4 coins) took 1.5 seconds. Which sentence do the results support?
opts: Canopy size changes the fall, and so does the load
Only the load changes the fall
Only the canopy size changes the fall
items.why: A and B differ only in canopy size, and the times differ. B and C differ only in load, and the times differ. So both matter.

items.p: How does each change affect the drag on a plane?
items: Painting the plane a different colour
items.a: as given
items.why: Drag grows with speed and with extra parts sticking out. Thin air high up reduces it. A colour does not change how air flows.

items.p: At 10 kilometres up, the air is about ____ as dense as the air at the ground.
a: a third
one third
a third as dense
items.why: At 10 kilometres the air is about one third as dense, so jets meet much less drag.

items.p: A flock of 8 birds takes turns to lead. Each bird leads for 3 minutes before going to the back. How many minutes pass before every bird has led once?
items.why: 8 birds with 3 minutes each is 8 times 3, which is 24 minutes.

items.p: Match each clue to what it tells you.
pairs: A card hangs far out in a fan's wind
the shape has a lot of drag
A ribbon hangs still just behind a book in the wind
the air behind a blunt shape can be calm
Smoke keeps curling after a card stops
moving air carries on after the thing has passed
A parachute with more coins lands sooner
a heavier load needs more drag to balance it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each clue shows one idea: shape and drag, the wake, the air carrying on, and the balance of drag and weight.

items.p: Which one is not a flap that steers a plane? Rudder, aileron, elevator, propeller.
items.a: The propeller, because it makes thrust to push the plane forward. The other three are flaps that change how the air pushes on the plane.
items.why: The rudder, aileron and elevator steer. A propeller pulls or pushes the plane through the air.

items.p: The swirling air behind a big plane stops the moment the plane has passed.
items.why: False. The whirls behind the wing tips keep moving for minutes. This is why planes wait before they use the same runway.

items.p: Two raindrops fall from the same cloud. One is big and one is small. Which one lands first?
opts: The big one, because it reaches a higher steady speed
The small one, because it is lighter
They land together
items.why: A bigger drop is heavier for its surface, so it needs more drag to balance it. It falls at a higher steady speed than a small one.

items.p: Put these in order, for a skydiver who falls and then opens a parachute.
a: She falls and speeds up until drag equals her weight
She falls at about 200 kilometres an hour
She opens the parachute and the drag jumps up
She slows to a new, much slower steady speed
items.why: Opening the canopy makes the drag much bigger than her weight, so she slows until drag equals weight again, at a much lower speed.

items.p: Draw a card swished through smoke. Show the smoke before the swish, and the whirls after the card has stopped.
items.a: A thin straight line of smoke, then a second drawing with the line bent into curls and spirals beside the card, which is held still.
items.why: The card moves the air, and the moving air carries on after the card has stopped. The whirls show that.

items.p: Why do jets climb to 10 kilometres even though it takes fuel to climb?
items.a: The air up there is thin, so there is much less drag. The jet saves more fuel by flying with less drag than it spends on climbing.
items.why: A strong answer says that the thin air means less drag at the same speed, so less thrust and less fuel are needed to cruise.

items.p: Asha, Bilal and Pooja plan to cycle 30 kilometres into a headwind in a line. Asha is the strongest rider.

views.says: I am the strongest, so I should lead the whole way.
Let us all take turns, so no one gets too tired.
The front rider works hardest. A short turn at the front, then a rest at the back, keeps the whole group fast.

items.ask: Whose plan will get the group there fastest, and why? What would you change if the wind blew from behind?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks the plan with turns, because the front rider works hardest, and says that a tailwind makes the front much less important.
items.why: The rider in front pushes the air aside. The riders behind feel less push, so rotating the lead spreads out the hardest job.

items.p: A designer wants a new bus to use less fuel on a long road. What advice about shape and speed would you give her, and why?
items.a: Make the front rounded and the back gently tapered, so the air flows smoothly and the wake is small. Drive at a moderate speed, because the drag grows with the square of the speed.
items.why: Drag depends on shape and on the square of the speed. A streamlined body and a lower speed both reduce drag.

items.p: Why can a plane not fly at 150 kilometres above the Earth?
opts: There is not enough air for the wings to push down
The Sun is too hot
Gravity stops at that height
items.why: Wings make lift by pushing air down. At 150 kilometres there is almost no air, so wings do nothing.

items.p: At everyday speeds, the shape with the least drag has a sharp, pointed front.
items.why: False. The best shape is rounded at the front and tapered at the back, like a teardrop.

items.p: A friend says: Bigger raindrops fall faster than small ones. Is she right? Say why.
items.a: Yes. A bigger drop is heavier for the size of its surface, so it needs more speed before drag equals its weight. It reaches a higher steady speed.
items.why: A strong answer says that the steady speed depends on the balance of drag and weight, and a bigger drop has a higher steady speed.

quiz.p: Which of these makes the drag on a moving thing bigger?
opts: Going faster
Turning off the engine
Making the front more rounded
quiz.why: Drag grows quickly with speed. A rounded, smooth front reduces drag, and turning off the engine does not change the push of the air.

quiz.p: A car goes from 30 kilometres an hour to 60. About how does the air drag change?
opts: It becomes about 4 times bigger
It stays the same
It doubles
quiz.why: Twice the speed means about four times the drag, because there is twice as much air each second, hit twice as hard.

quiz.p: A paper ball and a flat sheet of the same paper are dropped together. The ball lands first. What is the reason?
opts: The flat sheet has more drag
The ball is heavier
Gravity pulls the ball more
quiz.why: The paper is the same, so the weight is the same. The flat sheet faces more air, so its drag balances its weight at a lower speed.

quiz.p: The same parachute is dropped with 1 coin, and then with 4 coins. What happens?
opts: The 4-coin one falls faster, but not four times as fast
The 4-coin one falls four times as fast
They fall at the same speed
quiz.why: A heavier load needs more drag to balance it, so it falls faster. But the speed grows only with the square root of the weight, so four times the weight gives about twice the speed.

quiz.p: You want to find out if canopy size changes how fast a parachute falls. What must stay the same?
opts: The load, the drop height and the material
The size of the canopy
The colour of the room
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes, and all the others stay the same. Here the canopy changes, and the load, height and material are kept the same.

quiz.p: A paper plane keeps climbing steeply, stalls, and falls. What is a good fix?
opts: Bend the back edges of the wings down a little
Bend the back edges of the wings up
Fold the nose upwards
quiz.why: The nose is rising too much. Bending the back edges down pushes the back of the wings up, which pushes the nose down.

quiz.p: An arrow has feathers at its back. What is the job of the feathers?
opts: They add drag at the back, which keeps the point forward
They make the arrow heavier
They make the arrow spin
quiz.why: Feathers add drag at the back, so if the arrow turns sideways the air pushes it back in line, like a shuttlecock's feathers.

quiz.p: A pilot wants to roll a plane to the right. What does the pilot do with the ailerons?
opts: Raises the right aileron and lowers the left
Raises both ailerons
Turns the rudder
quiz.why: The wing with its aileron up lifts less and goes down. Raising the right aileron lowers the right wing, so the plane rolls right.

quiz.p: How does a plane go round a bend in the sky?
opts: It banks, and the tilted lift pulls it round
It points its rudder like a boat
It stops its engine
quiz.why: A plane tilts its wings, and part of the lift then pulls it sideways, round a curve. A cyclist leans in the same way.

quiz.p: A bird flies a little behind and to the side of another bird in a V. What helps her?
opts: The rising air from the wing tip of the bird in front
The bird in front pulling her
The wind from behind
quiz.why: The front bird leaves air rising just outside her wing tip. The bird behind can catch that air and save energy.

quiz.p: Why can a small insect fall from a table and be unhurt?
opts: She has a lot of skin for her weight, so air slows her fall
Gravity is weaker for small things
Insects have very strong bones
quiz.why: A small body has more skin for each bit of weight than a big one. The air slows her fall so much that she lands gently.

quiz.p: Why does a jet use less fuel at 10 kilometres up than at 1 kilometre, flying at the same speed?
opts: The air is thinner, so the drag is smaller
Gravity is zero
The jet is lighter
quiz.why: At 10 kilometres the air is about a third as dense, so the drag is much smaller, and the engines have less to fight.

open_questions.q: Can anyone predict exactly how the swirling air behind a moving thing will behave?
open_questions.why_open: The equations for moving air are well known, but nobody can solve them exactly for swirling, turbulent air. Whether they always have smooth answers is a million-dollar prize problem.

open_questions.q: How much energy does a V really save for each kind of bird?
open_questions.why_open: Measurements on ibises and pelicans show a saving, but it has been measured for very few kinds of birds, and seeing each other may matter too.

open_questions.q: How do tiny insects steer so well in air that feels thick to them?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists film them with very fast cameras. They still do not understand all the tricks that wings, hairs and tiny muscles use.

open_questions.q: Could a plane ever steer like a bird, by changing the shape of the whole wing?
open_questions.why_open: Engineers are testing wings that bend and twist smoothly, but nobody yet knows if they can be strong, safe and light enough for big planes.

open_questions.q: How do bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas, where the air is so thin?
open_questions.why_open: Trackers show they fly in a swooping pattern, but scientists are still working out how their bodies make enough power in air with so little oxygen.

Why do raindrops not hurt when they land, though they fall from so high?

maths.problem: In the Parachute Races, parachute B took 2.8, 2.6 and 2.7 seconds to fall. Work out the average time.
maths.explain: Add the times: 2.8 plus 2.6 plus 2.7 is 8.1. Divide 8.1 by 3 to get 2.7 seconds.
maths.context: In the Parachute Races, you time each parachute three times and find the average.
maths.why_maths: One drop can be spoilt by a gust, so the average of three drops is a fairer number to compare.

maths.problem: A cyclist rides into the wind at 10 kilometres an hour, then at 30. Twice the speed makes about four times the drag. How many times bigger is the drag at 30 than at 10?
maths.explain: 30 is 3 times 10. The drag grows with the square of the speed, so it is 3 times 3, which is 9 times.
maths.context: You have learned that drag grows faster than speed.
maths.why_maths: Squaring a number lets you predict how much harder the wind pushes when you go faster.

maths.problem: A big raindrop falls from a cloud 1,800 metres up at a steady 9 metres each second. How long does it take to land? Give the answer in minutes and seconds.
maths.explain: 1,800 divided by 9 is 200 seconds. 200 seconds is 3 minutes (180 seconds) and 20 seconds.
maths.context: A raindrop stops speeding up when its drag equals its weight, and then falls at a steady speed.
maths.why_maths: A steady speed makes the sum easy: distance divided by speed gives the time.

maths.problem: The 1-coin parachute lands 2 metres down in 2.6 seconds. Four times the weight gives about twice the speed. About how long would the 4-coin parachute take to fall the same 2 metres?
maths.explain: Twice the speed means half the time. Half of 2.6 is 1.3 seconds.
maths.context: In the Parachute Races, you drop the same parachute with 1 coin and with 4 coins.
maths.why_maths: Ratio sums let you predict a result before you test it, and then check if you were right.

maths.problem: The small canopy is 20 centimetres by 20 centimetres. The big canopy is 40 centimetres by 40 centimetres. How many times bigger is the area of the big canopy?
maths.explain: The small one is 20 times 20, which is 400 square centimetres. The big one is 40 times 40, which is 1,600. 1,600 divided by 400 is 4.
maths.context: In the Parachute Races, the big canopy is twice as long and twice as wide as the small one.
maths.why_maths: Drag depends on the area facing the air, so working out the area tells you how much more air the big canopy catches.

maths.problem: In the Steer a Paper Plane test, the planes landed at average distances of 4 steps for the plane with no bends, 2 steps for both edges up and 3 steps for both edges down. How much further did the plane with no bends go than the one with both edges up?
maths.explain: 4 take away 2 is 2 steps. The plane with no bends went 2 steps further than the plane with both edges up.
maths.context: In the Steer a Paper Plane test, you throw planes with different bends and note where they land.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the average distances shows how much each bend changed the flight.

maths.problem: A flock of 6 flamingos takes turns to lead. Each leads for 2 minutes at a time. They fly for 60 minutes. How many times does each bird lead?
maths.explain: One full round takes 6 times 2, which is 12 minutes. 60 divided by 12 is 5 rounds, so each bird leads 5 times.
maths.context: Birds in a line take turns at the front, because the front bird works hardest.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the flight into rounds shows that taking turns shares the hardest job equally.

maths.problem: One cubic metre of air at the ground has a mass of about 1.2 kilograms. At 10 kilometres up, the air is about a third as dense. What is the mass of a cubic metre of air up there?
maths.explain: A third of 1.2 is 1.2 divided by 3, which is 0.4 kilograms.
maths.context: Jets fly high, where the air is thin and the drag is smaller.
maths.why_maths: A fraction of the ground value tells you how much thinner the air is, and therefore how much less drag a jet faces.

maths.problem: A skydiver falling flat reaches about 55 metres each second. How many metres is that in one hour, and how many kilometres?
maths.explain: There are 3,600 seconds in an hour. 55 times 3,600 is 198,000 metres. Divide by 1,000 to get 198 kilometres.
maths.context: A skydiver stops speeding up when drag equals her weight, at a steady speed.
maths.why_maths: Changing metres each second into kilometres an hour lets you compare her speed with a car or a train.

maths.problem: Your cup wind meter turns 14 times in 30 seconds in the wind of a fan on medium. How many turns would it make in 10 minutes at that speed?
maths.explain: 10 minutes is 20 half-minutes. 14 times 20 is 280 turns.
maths.context: In the Cup Wind Meter project, you count the turns of the cups in 30 seconds.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a short count to a longer time is how weather stations turn quick counts into long-term wind records.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1752, the French mathematician Jean le Rond d'Alembert used the best mathematics of his day to work out what happens when a smooth object moves through a perfectly smooth, slippery fluid. His sums said the fluid would push on the front and the back of the object by the same amount, so the object would feel no drag at all. Everyone knew this was wrong, because a cannonball in air slows down. For over 150 years, the sums and the real world disagreed. People called it d'Alembert's paradox. In 1904, the German engineer Ludwig Prandtl gave the answer in a talk at a maths congress in Heidelberg. Real air is slightly sticky. A very thin layer of it clings to the surface of a moving object. Behind a blunt shape, that layer peels away into a messy wake, and this wake is where much of the drag comes from. Prandtl watched the wake form in a small water channel that he built, with bits of shiny mica floating in the flow.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean le Rond d'Alembert and Ludwig Prandtl
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The neat mathematics said that a smooth object in a smooth fluid would feel no drag. The sums left out the thin sticky layer of air, and Prandtl's experiment showed that this layer, and the wake it makes, is where drag comes from.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Parachute Races: the fall times are estimates from the usual sums for a polythene canopy. Expect about 2 seconds for the small canopy and 3 to 4 for the big one, about 2 for the big one with 4 coins and under 1 for the scrunched ball. A canopy that folds up counts as a failed drop and is repeated. A stopwatch adds about a fifth of a second of error, so the steps ask for the average of three drops. Steer a Paper Plane: the usual result is that both back edges bent up make the nose rise, both bent down make it dive, and one up and one down turn the plane towards the wing with the flap up. Results depend on a level, gentle throw, so the steps say what to do if a plane behaves oddly. The Card in the Fan: the card should swing a clear 10 to 30 centimetres on a low fan setting. The open cup and the flat card are blown about the same, and the cup's rounded back much less. Whirls Behind a Spoon and Swish in the Smoke need a still room and a thin sprinkle of pepper or a thin ribbon of smoke. If the whirls are faint, move more slowly or more quickly, and try again. Smoke is skipped for anyone with breathing trouble. Straw Hoop Glider: the small hoop goes in front. The result with the hoops turned round has not been tried, so the steps say to write what is seen. Cup Wind Meter: the cups must all face the same way or it will not spin. At everyday speeds drag grows with the square of the speed, so doubling speed gives about four times the drag.
